Vibroverb is one of the most sought-after vintage Fender amps, mainly due to SRV having 2 & Mark Knopfler played a ’63 brownface model

Due to low production numbers & their use by Stevie Ray Vaughan, 1964 (blackface) Vibroverbs have become highly collectible. SRV acquired 2 1964 blackface Vibroverbs in the late 70s, or early 80s, at 2 different times & locations, that somehow had sequential serial numbers. They were also modified by Cesar Diaz in many ways”

“SRV’s musical influence made the Fender Vibroverb the most sought after & hyped of all Fender amps. He played many other amps too, Super Reverb, Dumble & Marshalls. In studio, he used dozens of amps that were thrown at him. For some reason, Vibroverb has become the most famous & is now widely associated with his signature tone (though you can reproduce his tone with most Fender amps & the right speakers). Since Fender didn’t continue the Vibroverb after CBS takeover in 1965, likely because players didn’t desire 1×15” amps at that time, there’s only a few blackface Vibroverb amps out there. Given the hype & popularity, these few Vibroverbs are extremely valuable & collectible. So, what’s so special with the Vibroverb? 1st, the 15” speaker sets it apart from most guitar amps. While most guitar amps have multiple 10” & 12” speakers, Vibroverb came with 1 big Jensen C15n or JBLd130f, the last one with an aluminum dust cap & can be hard to tame. Otherwise, the blackface Vibroverb is very similar to the other black/silverface AB763 Fender amps. In fact, there aren’t any different features or technical improvements that justifies its popularity, it’s all about emotions. But that’s what music is all about: emotions”

Vibroverb belongs to the 6L6 Fender family. It’s powerful & loud, but in a different way vs 10” & 12” amps. It didn’t sell very well in 64-65. Players probably thought the amp was suited for bass amps, we’re not sure. It did score among steel guitar players at the time. The 15” speakers are firm in bass & have lots of sparkle, but most importantly, they have an enormous spread, carrying lower mids to anyone on stage. Mid freqs is exactly what you need on stage in an electrical band. The mids blend in nicely with bass, drums, piano & horns. It won’t interfere with the bass like a 4×10” setup does. Of course, it’s a matter of taste, but a guitar tone with strong mids contributes to a rich overall melodic footprint in an electrical band”

(Blackface era) Vibroverb was given the new blackface cosmetics & somewhat different circuitry (AA763). Still rated at 40w, the new design possessed the new blackface “optical coupler” vibrato circuit (in place of tweed-style vibrato found in its predecessor) & a bright switch. Gone also were the 2 10” Oxford speakers, in their place was a 1x15”. Both JBL & Jensens used, depended what was on hand at time of production

The blackface Vibroverb has 6L6 power tubes, low & high inputs, a Normal & Bright channel. It has Volume, Bass & Treble controls & Bright switch, plus reverb & vibrato controls. The Bright switch is engaged only in the AB model.
Fractal models of Fender amps always based on High input on amp. For Low input equivalent, set Input Trim to 0.5

notes: From Beatles to nowadays rock stars, everybody plays VOX amps: Brian May, The Edge, Rory Gallagher, Radiohead, Kings of Leon, Ritchie Blackmore etc. Did you know that the famous James Bond theme was recorded on an AC15? & for some divine reason, VOX is the tone of choice in P&W
The AC15 was developed before the AC30. The AC15 simply was not loud enough so VOX made a louder version: the AC30

“The Vox AC30 garnered more attention for years, but in this age of reduced stage volumes & project-studio recording practices, the smaller AC15 has become even more desirable in some players’ estimation. Dick Denney’s creation benefited from several design elements that were specifically intended to flatter the voice of the electric guitar, rather than merely amplify it & these babies achieve that in spades. Plug into stout EF86 pentode preamp channel for creamy, milkshake-thick tones or ECC83 channel for more jangle & sparkle & you quickly hear what all the fuss is about.”
The AC15 & AC30 were rather dark amps, with a single tone control. The “Brian May” tone. The Top Boost circuit was added later, adding gain & Bass & Treble controls & the well-known VOX “chime”.
The VOX is often cited to be a Class A amp. I’ll quote Korg/VOX about the difference between Class A & Class A/B amps:
“In order to understand difference between these 2 types of amp designs (there are others), must 1st understand a little about tubes.

The most basic tube used as an amplifier consists of 3 elements: Cathode, Plate & Grid. The Cathode is heated (by the heater, another element in all tubes except in very old designs where the cathode is the heater) & forms a cloud of negatively charged electrons. The Plate has a positive charge that attracts the electrons. The Grid is the audio input to the tube & usually controls the flow of electrons.

Amplification happens when a signal is applied to the grid that allows for & controls how much current flows through to the plate. Because the signal voltage is relatively low & the plate voltage is relatively high (as supplied by the power supply), the small changes produced by the audio signal at the Grid appear much larger at the Plate, hence amplification.
In a Class A circuit, a positive voltage is applied to the Grid, which controls the flow of electrons. In this circuit design current is flowing at all times through the tube.

In a Class “AB” design a negative “bias” voltage is applied to the grid, which will cause the tube to “shut off” when the audio waveform is below a certain point. Meanwhile there is another tube & associated circuit that is turning on before the first one turns off & is reproducing the rest of the waveform. In short these two tubes share the job of reproducing the full audio waveform.
Each type of design has its advantages & disadvantages.”
Class A advantages are:
The tube is ready to amplify the signal at all times
Signal is instantaneously amplified because tube doesn’t have to “wake up” from a less than full operational state
30w “Class A” amp will sound louder than a 30w Class AB amp
Because current is max at all times, amp has smooth compression
Not a lot of headroom, as lower plate voltages used in Class A amps
Instantaneous amplification & smooth compression make an amp that is responsive to the touch: the amp feels good & playing it is a satisfying experience
Combined with EL84s in push-pull operation, amp will emphasize high order harmonics & sing
Class A disadvantages are:
Always Max current, means tubes are strained even without playing
Shorter tube life
Lower power rating vs Class AB amp with same tube configuration
Power transformer needs upgraded to handle high current demands
Class AB advantages:
Longer tube life because tubes are “idling” with lower Plate Current
Higher power ratings with the same tube configuration
More headroom
Tighter bass response
Less continuous demand on the power transformer.
Class A/B disadvantages:
Not as “responsive” vs Class A amp

“Vox isn’t really a Class amp, it’s a Class A push-pull with cathode bias. Some believe high bias condition is source of the amp’s famous immediate response & jangly high-end, though lack of negative feedback, minimal preamp circuit, simple low loss tone stack & output stage cathode biasing have a large role, if not larger”

AC15 runs on EL84 power tubes. Originally AC15 had an EF86 preamp tube in 1 channel & ECC83 (currently: ECC83/12AX7) in other. There’s no EF86 in current AC15/AC30 models, have to resort to boutique alternatives for that, like Matchless & Morgan
High & Low inputs per channel. If real amp has both, model always based on High. For Low equivalent, decrease Input Trim

VOX are no negative feedback amps. Negative feedback sends a bit of signal coming out of the amp back to power amp input. It cleans up tube distortion (causes loss of harmonics). If no negative fdbk, Damping is set to 0. Presence then becomes a Hi-Cut control.

Original AC15 had 2 channels. 1st provided a Vibravox effect (not modeled). Channel 2 had Volume & Cut control (Hi-Cut). Later models with Top Boost added Bass & Treble. Recent models have Normal & Top Boost channels & additional options (Bright, MV,etc.)
Not disclosed amp model based on, other than has Top Boost circuit
“AC30 has no negative feedback, which is why it sounds way it does”
A VOX typically feeds Alnico Blue or greenbacks. Blue refers to color of speaker’s metal. Alnicos are often used when bright tones needed

“Class-A amps (like AC30) don’t actually exhibit much power supply sag, as they’re Class-A (or nearly). Tubes biased hot, so when 1 tube conducts more, other conducts less & net supply current doesn’t change much. Contrast with Class-AB, when 1 tube conducts, other goes into cutoff, causing net increase in supply current & supply sag. What Class-A amps do exhibit is cathode squish. Cap on cathodes charges up & shifts bias point, reduces gain, acts as sorta unique compressor, amp opens up & crossover distortion increases”

“In a tube power amp, lows & highs distort 1st, boosted by speaker impedance, causes sound to become more midrangey & focused. Then, as signal decays, sound gets fuller & less midrangey. One of most important things in way tube amp operates & responsible for unique, pleasing OD behavior & why they became gold-standard, also what makes AC30 so unique. Have no negative feedback so lows & highs are fully boosted by speaker impedance. When driven hard, they get focused. Backing off volume they become full & chimey”

AC30 has High & Low inputs per channel. If original amp has both inputs, the amp model is always based on the High input. To get the equivalent of the Low input, decrease Input Trim in the amp model.

“JCM800s sound better with hot bias IMO. Problem is plate voltage is too high, so when setting bias higher, dissipation goes up & tube life is shortened. IMO they should’ve made plate voltage around 420V, would allow hotter bias with longer tube life, at expense of little less volume, but JCM800s are ungodly loud anyways, so...“

“Interference is due to treble peaking used in design. JCM800s have quite a bit of treble boost. When 1st attacking string, note is unpitched, basically a brief explosion of noise. Treble boosting amps upper freqs of noise burst, which is what’s heard. However, when playing in a loud mix, that treble boosting helps sound cut. Modern designs use more carefully crafted treble boosting to retain cut, but tame some attack harshness. Accomplished typically by putting capacitor in parallel with plate resistor(s), rolls off a few kHz, preserves treble boost in upper midrange, but softens attack. I believe SLO100 was 1 of 1st amps to do this. Can see this in Axe-Fx as Triode Freq parameters. Can soften JCM800 attack by lowering Triode Freq values. Most modern hi-gain designs use some form of HF rolloff like this. Another reason is JCM800s use relatively low amounts of negative fdbk (why they’re so loud), causes treble boost in power amp. Increase Damping parameter to increase negative fdbk”
“Designed to get character from power amp distortion. If you don’t push power amp, all you’re hearing is preamp (voiced to be trebly). Power amp then compresses highs/gets fatter”
(Move MV post-phase inverter)”It’s called PPI MV/Lar-Mar Mod”

Has raw tone, slightly glassy & hollow in a good way. Crank it & enjoy pure British power amp distortion. Wanna hear a Hiwatt in its full glory? Listen to The Who’s Live At Leeds, quoted by some as best live rock recording of all time (Pete Townsend used CP103, based on DR103). Then there’s David Gilmour, Pink Floyd’s master of tone, who’s played Hiwatt all his life.

“The amp that started it all. DR103 has proved itself as cornerstone of such a huge variety of acts that’s provided them all with platform on which to build their own, unique sounds. Amp kicks out such pure, powerful tone it really compliments pedals put through it vs competes with them, like some other amps, yet has rich, classic ‘British’ tone, which stands out distinctively, particularly when amp’s cranked. Dual channel preamp with high/low sensitivity inputs & normal/bright options on each. Volume controls for each channel & master volume control. 3 band EQ; bass, middle & treble. 4xEL34s at power stage, either 4xECC83s or 3xECC83s & 1xECC81 (tighter sound) at preamp stage.” – Hiwatt

“Hiwatts were marketed as high-end amp & indeed their quality in construction, from use of premier Partridge transformers, to exquisite attention, to detail being made in electronic wiring & assembly, quickly further enhanced Hiwatt’s rep. Even die-hard/loyal Marshall enthusiasts have to admit the construction quality of early Hiwatts were vastly superior to Marshalls. Person responsible for this was Hiwatt’s Chief Tech Harry Joyce, who oversaw construction of these amps, built & signed many of them himself. Harry Joyce was a military-certified wiring tech & as a result, all Hiwatt produced during Harry Joyce era were produced at military-spec levels. Military specs required products made be wired in such a way components would be easily accessible & wiring itself would remain “clean”, to allow quick/efficient repairs of military equipment in the field. Looking inside a Hiwatt chassis, this attention to “Mil-Spec’s” evident, attention to detail was a primary reason Hiwatt production was limited to 40 amps a month.

Most famous Hiwatt was Custom 100 DR103. 100w output compared to Marshall Super Lead is quite different. Hiwatt DR103 is notably louder, can run much cleaner vs 100w Marshalls if needed & have tremendous headroom. Playing a Hiwatt at loud volume is an experience. When I played through one the 1st time, all of a sudden, my Marshalls felt thin in comparison. Hiwatt are loud, punchy, rich, with even-ordered harmonics & ballsy as hell! I can think of no better example of the epitome of clean/lush tube tone. OD is certainly available when Hiwatt’s pushed, but must be acquired by use of higher-gain “brilliant” channel & high-output pickup helps further. “Normal” channel’s voiced to stay clean & powerful at all levels. Another benefit to DR103’s tone & design was its inclusion of tone controls that actually seemed to respond with much wider range vs other amps of the time. Bass response could be bassy, mids added strong punch & wide range of treble/presence controls delivered all upper freqs & sibilants desired”
Hiwatt creates a great clean tone. Glassy but different from a VOX, just listen to Pink Floyd

18.controls: Gain, Treble, Bass, Mid, Presence, Master, Pull Bright, GEQ, Pentode/Triode switch, Class-A/Simul-Class switch, Voicing switch (Mid Gain/Harmonics), Variac
notes: Rhythm 1 feels bouncy & shimmers with freshness
Rhythm 1 channel, the clean tone, stays really clean for the most part of its Gain range. Use Bright switch for Pull Bright

RHYTHM 1 GAIN CONTROL: Setting RHYTHM 1 mode adjusts input sensitivity for clean RHYTHM mode. With most guitars, mode stays clean until ~8 where it begins to OD. Use R1 MASTER to control loudness if you want slight OD at low volumes. Mode carefully designed to provide great rhythm sounds, from best of vintage, Fender-type (clean or solo) to more modern, shimmering “funk rhythm” sound. Be sure to try this mode played really loud, you’ll love it for blues/rock

PULL BRIGHT: Adds shimmer & sparkle to sound when activated, the amount of added brightness varies with R1 GAIN setting: more brights at lower settings, less at higher. For super shimmer: GAIN ~3-4 & BRIGHT pulled out. For most naturally balanced sound: Run GAIN ~6-7 with BRIGHT pulled

RHYTHM 1 TREBLE: Control dials in predominate tonal characteristic. 0-3 range: Dark, warm jazz tone. Most common settings are in 5-7 range & note how overall gain of mode increases with higher TREBLE control settings, as so much energy of musical spectrum is channeled through this control. True of all modes, has 3 separate TREBLE controls

R1 PRESENCE: Adjusts freqs higher than those found on TREBLE control. There’s many different sounds RHYTHM 1 can produce, experiment using guitar & your ears. Try settings like low on TREBLE control, high on PRESENCE control & the opposite, as an experiment, both with & without BRIGHT switch. Notice too that when playing very loud, higher PRESENCE settings help cut through the background wash of cymbals. Don’t forget to turn RHYTHM 1 up loud & blow, it’s a great OD sound too

R1 MASTER: Adjusts signal level of RHYTHM 1 mode, allows running various settings of RHYTHM 1 GAIN, while still controlling overall RHYTHM 1 volume via MASTER. Important because of striking tonal differences BRIGHT switch makes at lower & higher settings of gain & because high GAIN control settings are useful for producing “onset of clip” distortion sounds

R1+R2 BASS & R1+R2 MID: Shared tone controls. Because of internal circuitry changes, which occur when switching modes, you’ll find R1’s optimum setting works well for RHYTHM 2. Effect of these 2 tone controls is largely determined by setting of TREBLE controls. Only when TREBLE is set very low (or off) are BASS & MID controls really strong, at normal TREBLE settings, their effect is greatly diminished & serve mainly to round out & fill up overall tone. Setting BASS control too high can result in unwanted flubbiness, especially in RHYTHM 2. Recommended setting for BASS control is 0-3 & for MID control 4-7

(Rhythm Green) With very high GAIN values, may need to reduce MASTER a lot. Its Dynamic response makes it the hottest, output-wise

“More vintage, old Blackface style circuit. A beyond-vintage clean sound, with bubbly, elastic highs & big breathy lows. This mode shines at many other settings too. As GAIN & MIDRANGE controls are increased, 5.5-7.5, a whole new flavor appears. This hotter region performs as a killer driving, yet still clean, rhythm sound. Bold & pushed, this dynamic range of tones works great for Blues rhythm grooves or more aggressive “alternative” clean parts or lines. This is probably the most powerful & widest of possible rhythm sounds aboard TriAxis, perfect for when it’s your turn in the spotlight. Go ahead. Crank it! Rhythm Green loves to rock.

This is the sound that helped put Boogies in the hands of widely acclaimed guitar heroes of the 70’s/early 80’s, when Blues/Fusion changed & revoiced rock with tasty medium gain sounds. This circuit was inspired by the classic 4x10 Fender Bassman & later redefined in Mark 1 Boogies. Classic, bare-bones, roots players will love how well this setting responds to pickup output. Virtuosos of the volume knob can take or leave foot switching in favor of a circuit that lets them ride gain from their guitar. Rhythm Green works extremely well for this & will surprise even the most hardcore vintage heads.

GAIN control has a Dynamic “Bright” circuit built into it. At low Gain settings, upper harmonics pass freely through this control, producing the sweetest, brightest sounds. The more GAIN is increased, the less of these upper harmonics pass through & warmer the sound becomes. GAIN all the way up virtually removes these freqs from the mix & may want to use PRESENCE to put some of them back. Use MIDRANGE with BASS to balance warmth with upper harmonics at low Gain settings & reduce PRESENCE until you achieve desired blend”
For a long time, Petrucci relied on a couple TriAxis units to get his favorite MkIIC+ tones on the road, as did Metallica

“Mesa claims it’s based on IIC+, but it’s different. Bright cap is different, mid resistor is much greater, source impedance of drive “pot” is different, etc”

“On our reference Triaxis (both of them), Presence control does nothing for the Clean & LD1 modes. Model’s Presence knob is therefore the Power Amp Presence” & “When using the LD1 modes the Presence control doesn’t do anything & is as if the control were at 10”

“Triaxis used LDRs as variable resistance elements. There were resistor strings that were used to set the LDRs but those resistors weren’t in the signal path”

Presence control: “This usually regulates either brightness or negative feedback in the power section of amp. In the TriAxis a whole new approach to this circuit was taken. Actual dynamic feedback loop, compresses highs & upper treble freqs makes control 1st of its kind.

As PRESENCE is increased, more highs are allowed to pass. The lower the signal strength at input of this, the more highs pass through it. The lower region of PRESENCE dampens these high harmonics. Greater the signal strength at circuit input becomes, the darker the sound becomes. So, if you set PRESENCE high & pick softly (sending a small signal through PRESENCE circuit) highs will be very prominent in the mix.

If you decrease PRESENCE & pick harder (increasing signal strength at PRESENCE circuit input), high harmonics will be very subtle. In other words, it helps enhance whichever direction you’re trying to go in with your sound & does so dynamically! Most players love the way tube circuits react to subtle nuances in style, This control circuit takes that idea a few steps further. When you’re “going off” on the treble strings in a solo, you go for an expressive bend & lay hard into the note, TriAxis works with you! If you picked the note hard with PRESENCE set low, that note becomes bigger, rounder & more compressed.

Likewise, if you’re doing some low growling work on the bass strings & PRESENCE was set high, you could relax into this segment & let the control make the edge. Most everyone we know wishes their high notes could be fatter, low notes more discernible & articulate, highs where you need them, lack of highs where you don’t. Experience the way this dynamic control can enhance your playing, especially when soloing”
“It’s just speculating but the Presence circuit in the TriAxis may have been the inspiration for Fractal to develop the Dynamic Presence & Dynamic Depth parameters” - yek

“Added the “Bright” control to the Amp block. This high treble control is a shelving filter between the preamp & power amp & may be used to darken or brighten the output of the preamp. It also changes the load on the plate, which distorts the freq response a bit too. Presence should be set to 5.00, which is neutral”

“Back when I was testing IIC+’s every day in the burn-in room, I always thought the non-graphic amps had a certain attack & purity to the sound that amps with Graphic EQ on them just didn’t have. There was urgency & bold punch to the sound, they seemed tighter & more cohesive. Granted, we made far more amps with on-board EQ than without, probably 70% had EQ, but not many people had an opportunity to compare day-in/day-out as I did. EQ model had the shaping advantage, no doubt about it & certainly all sounds IIC+ are famous for were created with EQ being an integral part of that sound, but when it came to the straight sound, no EQ, non-graph model always got to me with its speed & authority. So it was that I came to be the obsessive/compulsive owner of no less than 8 of them. I hand picked these as being the best sounding amps for me, out of 1000s of IIC+ we made. Out of these 8 amps, I immediately found my favorite, which I dubbed “His Highness the C-ness”, which I used as a reference model to have our Chief Tech & Archival Guru Michael Bendinelli, copy exactly on the other 7. Everything was measured, scrutinized (pot values, resistors, caps, transformers swapped, etc.), duplicated, & in the end, all 8 sounded alike. In our endless comparisons of many original IIC+’s, both EQ & non-EQ samples, alongside this golden reference, we discovered that I wasn’t just Tone-dreaming. There’s actually a difference between EQ model & those non-EQ models. It all came down to a coupling capacitor at the end of the EQ circuit that feeds the driver. In the EQ model, it was a great big cap that let a lot of sub-low pass, slowing down the sound & making it fatter. In my amp, a non-EQ version, this cap was smaller & didn’t let as much sub-low through, which speeds up the sound & makes everything tighter & more urgent. There it was, a simple part, but it made all the difference in the time domain. Yet there were so many more of these slower, fatter sounding EQ versions out in the world many more people were used to hearing as their reference. It wouldn’t do well to set MARK V permanently to this faster, tighter way. Too many players would have a tough time adjusting & when they compared the 2 amps side by side, the V would sound faster & tighter yes, but also stripped of sub-low & therefore maybe not as fat in comparison to their trusty IIC+ Graphic model or MARK IV, which also had the bigger coupling cap” – Douglas Wes

“Pull Bright on Volume knob is classic Bright Cap, which engages a capacitor across the potentiometer. This is already modeled in the AxeFx via Bright Switch. Pull Bright on Lead Master knob engages a 0.22uF cap on cathode of last triode in the OD circuit. As there’s no switch for this in the AxeFx, it requires a separate model. Cathode caps are very common in tube amps. If value is large, stage has more gain & response is relatively flat. If value is small, stage has more gain at higher freqs. Amp designers use cathode caps to shape freq response. Caps in range of 0.1 to 1.0uF are commonly used to reduce bass response. A cathode cap works by decreasing amount of negative feedback through shunting higher freqs to ground, this reduced negative feedback, increases gain (& reduces linearity). FWIW the AxeFx is the only modeler I’m aware that actually models triodes using a feedback technique. Others use static waveshapers. AxeFx triode models incorporate feedback so if there’s a virtual cathode cap, stage is less linear in addition to having more gain”

23.power_tubes: 6L6 (deliver most powerful clean sounds along with richest distortion). Can also use:
notes: Lead channel, Voicing: Harmonics
1. Type 5881 (like 6L6, but just slightly less powerful, somewhat rounder, more vintage tone)

2. EL34+6L6 (for those seeking traditional British edge to their OD sounds. In Simul-Class, combo of 6L6’s & EL34’s produce louder, fatter sound, while retaining British edge. Expect clean sound to suffer a bit when EL34s are used)

famous for smooth high gain tones, endorsement by Petrucci

Lead channel, with Voicing set to Harmonics, & Pull Bright off. Use the FAT switch for Pull Fat. Presence Shift is available as a switch under Presence. This is the model you may want to select when playing loud

Like all MESA amps, Mark amps feature a LOT of knobs & switches. MESA states in the manual: “Every possible useful feature is included”. This can make them difficult to dial in for those who suffer from Option Anxiety, Parameter Paralysis or Agony of Choice. Also why modeling this amp requires a # of separate models
The Lead Mode is blistering high-gain focus
“Pull” controls are:
Rhythm 1: Bright
Rhythm 2: Fat (more gain) & Shift Presence (higher frequency area)
Lead: Fat (more gain), Bright (adds sizzle/gain) & Shift Presence (higher freqs)

Lead channel also has Voicing Switch, where Mid Gain delivers more gain (meant for low volume levels) & Harmonics sounds more balanced (meant for high volume levels) & an additional gain control (Lead Drive)
SETTING THE LEAD MODE:

LEAD GAIN: This control sets up input sensitivity for LEAD mode. More signal strength dialed in here, early in preamp, the more distortion will be available at the LEAD DRIVE control. Yet it isn’t necessary or recommended to turn LEAD GAIN fully up. Best results occur with settings in 8 range. As you approach Gain of 7, Lead sound becomes extremely focused, rich & smooth. Above 8 , total saturation occurs, reducing effectiveness of tone controls, causing increased “microphonics” & noise in preamp tubes. You’ll notice subtle shifts in distortion tonality by trying different mixes of LEAD GAIN & LEAD DRIVE. LEAD GAIN control incorporates a PULL FAT for thickening sound & saturating signal further. This pull shift lowers freq of the Treble, adding a boost in lower midrange. Try this shift for beefing up sound of weaker, stock pick-ups or simply for adding focus at virtually any setting of the GAIN control

There’s also some great singing, slightly distorted sounds that come from low settings of Gain & Drive with FAT pushed in. “Onset of Clip” & “threshold of distortion” are phrases often used to describe these sounds, which reveal the true blue beauty of the all-tube lineage

LEAD TREBLE: Control, along with RHYTHM 2’s PRESENCE should be worked with together to produce desired gain & brightness of mode. Setting TREBLE higher, as always, increases gain of mode & allows increased distortion & sustain. Lower settings allow MID & BASS controls to become more dominant adding warmth to sound.

LEAD BASS & LEAD MID: Both these controls add body & warmth without really affecting strength of signal. Merely dial in to liking but note that too much Bass combined with too high a LEAD GAIN setting will take away from tight, highly focused lead sound that this mode offers

LEAD DRIVE: Works in conjunction with LEAD GAIN to determine amount of sustain & OD. It’s not necessary or even recommended to run LEAD DRIVE way up in order to generate a sound that’s fully saturated, so try settings in 5-7 region. Higher settings tend to increase noise & squealing without really embellishing the sound or feel. Notice this control comes on very rapidly at low settings, then changes only gradually throughout rest of its rotation. Familiarize with point which represents the beginning or “threshold” of OD, it creates an expressive distortion, that’s touch-sensitive to picking dynamics, providing harmonics that stay glued to the fundamental note. You’ll find lots of great sounds in 2-4 region

LEAD BRIGHT: Importance of switch is a must to understand. At low to medium playing volumes, it adds desirable sizzle & gain in highs to the OD sound & contributes to a “big easy feeling” too. At high volumes, can cause real problems, such as excess squealing & noise. At high volumes it’s often not necessary to supplement the LEAD mode’s natural gain because the power amp will also be going into OD. Keep in mind how Boogie’s cascading gain works: there’s several amp stages in a row with “gain” controls at all crucial points in between, so you can produce enormous amounts of amp gain at low volumes. MARK IV is capable of playing very loud as well, but it isn’t feasible to play with high gain & high volume simultaneously, without causing squealing, feedback & excess noise. A Ferrari is a great car in tight corners & it’s wickedly fast on straightaway, but at some combination of speed & cornering it’ll spin-out. So will MARK IV!

So remember to balance “gain” with “volume”. In LEAD mode, a general guideline might be push in BRIGHT for loud playing & pull out BRIGHT at lower volumes. 12AX7 tubes will be much happier & so will your soundman! (Another switch similarly “dangerous” at high gain/high volume settings is LEAD VOICING switch, described later in this manual.)

LEAD PRESENCE & LEAD MASTER: Controls work similarly to those previously discussed. Note, adding lots of PRESENCE (which is extra gain in highest freq range) to high gain & high volume settings may aggravate spin-out of squealing & excess noise. LEAD PRESENCE control has a PULL SHIFT, which operates like R2 PRESENCE PULL SHIFT, reduces amount of low freqs & shifts range of Presence effect.

You may find that pulling out PRESENCE control gives better balance playing with a band, while pushing in PRESENCE has bigger & fatter sound for mic’ed up recording. When shift is pushed in & graphic EQ is set to “Classic V” setting, unholy amounts of tight, chunking bottom end are available. Give this setting a try for metal rhythm grooves.

GRAPHIC EQ: Setting up EQ is strictly a matter of personal taste & enjoyment, prepare to have some fun dialing in fine nuances of tonal shading, or going for outer extremes of weirdness! One setting recommended as a departure point is called “classic V”. It involves boosting lowest & highest freq sliders the most, boosting 240 & 2200 sliders somewhat less & cutting 750 center band

Can be as subtle or extreme as you want with this pattern & when you’re going for extremes, you’ll notice the 750 slider is by far the most crucial. Once you’ve boosted the other 4 bands, you’ll find that by adjusting only 750, you can determine the strength of the entire EQ effect. You’ll also notice that there’s a certain point where sound goes from max thrash to thin & buzzy. Your ears quickly become adjusted (addicted?) to this hyper-tone & when you switch EQ back out of the circuit, straight tone sounds to flat. Don’t worry! It’s just “hearing hangover”. 1992 was a crucial year for guitar-based rock music. Thrash metal peaked, hair metal evaporated, grunge went Platinum & guitar amp that’d soon eviscerate them all was about to inspire a new gen of players/producers to remake metal in its image.
Peavey’s engineers put finishing touches on the 5150, a new breed of high-gain guitar amp outfitted with 9 tubes, hyper-responsive tone stack & soon patented Resonance control, lynchpin to its tone

“In amp’s master section, Resonance alters damping factor around speaker’s resonant peak, so amp controls transient response of loudspeaker. “Defining attribute largely responsible for 5150 sound is fixed bias. Commonly described analog a car engine & its respective idle, 5150 bias was set to lower value (lower engine “idle”), resulted in Power Tubes running at lower energy, known as cold-biased. While electrical theory behind this can easily be examined/theoreticized, 5150 & configuration resulted in more controllable gain setting (ie. having more forgiving sonic range vs similar “hot-biased” configs. This engineering choice set 5150 up to intrinsically sound best with minimal change. Since tube-amps are still uncontested in music amps, far as tonal quality’s concerned, (see hard-clipping) optimal setting for tubes are when they’re pushed to natural distortion (ie. Increases in volume or Bells(dB). “IMO poor design, they exhibit a papery buzz. Problem with most cathode biased Class A amps is 1. aren’t really Class A (more like hot Class AB) & 2. Go into Class B operation when OD. Cathode capacitor charges up & bias point shifts dramatically, causes lotta crossover distortion (papery buzz), worse on lower notes as lower notes have more energy & charge cap more. Probably reason Leo Fender switched to fixed bias amps with negative feedback. Fixed bias is just that, bias point’s fixed so amp doesn’t shift into Class B operation when overdriven (not as much anyways, depends on bias circuit, grid stoppers, etc). Negative feedback linearizes amp & reduces crossover distortion (at expense of gain). That’s why buzzing went away when you increased negative fdbk. Crossover distortion’s a unique sound. For cleaner sounds tends to be objectionable. For OD sounds some find it desirable. EVH ostensibly liked his amps biased cold for some crossover distortion. There’s even some amps that have circuits to intentionally generate crossover distortion, some distortion pedals also do this. Lowering Cathode Resistance reduces crossover distortion, keeps amp in Class A operation longer but tubes run hotter & don’t last as long, it’s not a problem with virtual amps though. I forget actual values, but I’m pretty certain if you look at Cathode Resistance value for those amps, it’s pretty high, means amps are biased somewhat cold to begin with & shift to very cold when overdriven. Then there’s shared vs. split cathode. If you look at schematics online, Maz-38 is shared cathode. I could never get model to sound exactly like our ref amp. Finally I traced the entire circuit & our particular amp is a split cathode. Soon as I changed model to split cathode, it was spot on. This is not exposed to user though (there’s a hidden shared/split switch). Our particular amp says Humbucker in chassis. Not sure if difference in cathode circuit’s due to Dr. Z likes split cathode for humbucking guitars?” - FAS

I wanted an amp that’d have little more gain vs JCM-800, but with character of Plexi, without fizz or harsh upper mid/lower treble freqs. Remember this was BEFORE anyone had even degooped or documented Bluesmaster style circuit & only thing Shad was building was his post count at AmpGarage, asking about Dumble circuits. I find it amazing it took guys years to catch on with moving pots to front. Does require bit more thought than just moving pots as ranges of those trimmers Dumble used is impractical when used as front panel controls (they weren’t really intended to be). Do also agree that from pure tone standpoint, nothing on front panel is always gonna be better. JB100 model’s basically an OD2 with entire OD circuit on the board, with predefined filters made up of quality components, without adjustment through fragile trimmers. OD2 was never designed to be put side by side in a Dumble clone fest, in some guys living room with everyone playing their best Ford licks, it was designed to be used on stage, for guys playing in cover/blues/wedding/classic rock bands. Separate EQ & tube driven effects loop were added for that situation. I’ve always tried to avoid that association as much as possible, as average Dumble lover is typically looking for a particular set of tones that may/may not be found in this amp. Early customer interaction made me wanna ensure people knew it wasn’t a tonal clone of Dumble, to avoid misunderstandings. OD-2 isn’t best amp for those tones, I agree, but Dumble or clone doesn’t really do fast dampened power chords like OD-2 does either, it’s much more suited for blues & classic rock, not Ford/Carlton thing. Bear in mind, average player’s looking for function/tone, not particular design architecture. Fact I used HRM style circuit obviously (& unfortunately) placed me in Dumble category. But 2500 amps later, not really seen that way anymore, as CA’s always had their own thing going on tonally, much more in a modded Marshall vein. Newer models, like Triptik 2, have nothing in common with any Dumble, not even cathode driven tonestack. For anyone that’s played real Dumbles, there’s a certain thing (heard more in clean channel) that’s uniquely his signature, certain swirl to clean tone always in his amps. However, amp doesn’t OD anywhere near what I like when pushed hard. For me, I’d rather focus on that tone in a Plexi. Who knows what original guy he modded this for wanted. “Only amps with bright cap on MV are Dumbles & their various derivatives. Was/is done to compensate for lack of buffer for fx loop. Same idea as bright cap on guitar’s volume knob. Crude. FWIW, this is a terrible loop design, but “it’s a Dumble” so it’s part of mystique. Supro’s origins date to the pre-electric guitar days & formation of the National Resophonic guitar company around 1926, with roots in the resonator guitars that became a blues tone standard prior to amplification. National & Dobro merged in early ’30s to form Valco & Supro. Soon, Valco-made Supro amps were tearing it up on Chicago’s south-side scene, establishing a tone that’s been synonymous with gritty blues ever since. By the mid 60’s, Jimi Hendrix was playing a Supro Thunderbolt amp on tour with Little Richard & Isley Brothers. Few years later, Jimmy Page, inspired by the raw tones of Chicago blues scene, cut seminal Led Zeppelin tracks on a Supro Model 24 & so the chain of influence goes, full circle from Chicago blues, to London blues-rock, with Supro, the hip tone to beat

There’s a girth, depth & dimension to the tone of these old circuits that’s simply unattainable from other brands & a dynamic playing feel that definitely puts a smile on my face every time. Keep them clean & they’re sweet & rich, crank them up & even smaller Supro models issue a bold, furious roar that retains edge & cutting power amid heavy OD

“Dual-Tone 1×12 combo amp is the undeniable rock star of the mid 60’s Supro amp lineup. Vintage 1624T amps have been sought-after for decades, as they embody the most desirable aspects of Supro’s sound. As Dual-Tone volume knob is turned past noon, a fat & compressed clean tone evolves into an immediately recognizable grind that remains articulate & listenable, even when turned up to full blast

This 24w, 1×12 tube combo can easily be driven to glorious saturation at manageable gigging volume, while retaining exceptional clarity & bandwidth, at any level of gain. Amp’s unique mojo’s largely defined by 6973 power tubes in amp’s output stage. These robust 9-pin tubes were employed extensively in the mid- & low-power Supro amps made 50 years ago. 6973 tubes look like EL84s, but they deliver a distinctly American voice missing from the world of tube amps for far too long.

Dual-Tone’s linkable channels each sport volume & tone controls & a shared tremolo circuit. Plugging into IN 1+2 links both preamp channels in parallel for double input signal & doubled gain. This clever topology lets you hit the power amp hard as needed & even allows “channel switching” in its purest form, using a simple A/B switch

1964 RI Supro Dual-Tone’s vintage-correct, lightweight cab, with our custom 12” Supro speaker, kicks out surprisingly plump low end with the detailed midrange & high end articulation that defines Supro tone players have been chasing for decades. Loud enough to gig with a band, Dual-Tone’s the perfect small club/recording amp” – Supro

notes: “...Post-tone control gain circuit. With heralded veterans of this design, the MkIIB, IIC+, MkIII & MkIV, the rear-end lead legacy lives on, stronger than ever! It’s in LEAD 2 we celebrate these classic lead sounds & offer up a couple variations on the theme. Again, these are the more articulate & focused lead sounds. Some players that grew up playing non-MESA amps may find these dry & stiff initially, but have patience & you’ll come to enjoy these modes. There’s simply less “slop around note” in these modes, making them a sorta magnifying glass for inaccurate playing. Though at times they’re more revealing, you’ll find they hold up better in a mix & are much more behaved on a stage full of live mics. Usually they’re also much better for any kind of rhythmic high gain playing where you need urgent attack & tight cut-off points

The Green circuit’s taken directly from a MkIV Lead channel. Green is focused gain, uses the concept of the MkIV’s Mid Gain, a feature added in ‘89, to enhance attack & lower medium midrange “meat” of the sound. Enhancing this part of the spectrum, a rich, bold, yet singing quality is produced. Thick is the best way to describe its character, while Punchy accurately describes its attack. It does saturate the note fairly completely, especially at high gain settings, but the attack envelope is so right at lower gain settings, that roots players usually love this mode. Its’ thicker midrange punch really helps melody lines played on high strings, particularly high on the neck. With higher Gain & Drive settings, high notes soar & sing, yet don’t get too soupy to be heard in a big mix. Green is especially helpful in getting rid of unwanted fret buzz or other annoying idiosyncrasies of an instrument that may be set up wrong. Tends to cover up buzz leaving just the note with greater purity. This is most apparent when a weak single coil is used for soloing, the cure for this dilemma. It adds the needed freqs & gain is the steroid habit these weaklings need to deliver a bold lead voice. Mode of choice anytime needing to deliver a statement & don’t have the luxury of several tracks. It’s single note authority at its expressive best.
tips: As mentioned earlier in Lead 1 Red, GAIN setting in all modes is crucial to achieving the sound you’re looking for. Each mode has its’ magical optimum setting for this control, we can only give our view & a few factory settings to demonstrate our thinking on this. Ultimately, it varies for each mode, guitar, player, environment & on you to discover what fits a situation. In Lead 2. we’ve come to a simple rule of thumb to where we prefer GAIN to achieve the best blend of attack & tone quality. Try this 1st, then deviate from there in all Lead 2 modes. We like to see Gain at 7.0-7.5 (depends on instruments output) for lower gain blues sounds or very articulate medium gain solo sounds. When higher gain or straight up radical rock sound is in demand, GAIN 7.5-8.0 (again depends on pickup output) should be more than enough

With higher than recommended Gain settings, a flubby, indistinct attack occurs that the BASS control has difficulty removing. Lower than optimum Gain settings produces excessive high harmonic content, thins notes out & even add a buzzy quality to the sound”

notes: “This is Boogie. This mode is the sound that started the craze that became what is slanged as the “California” sound or the “LA” guitar tone. Lukather, Landau, Keaggy, Lynch, Gillis, Prince & Metallica catapulted this sound into the forefront of hit making guitar sounds throughout the 80s. Metallica continues to search high & low for pristine C+ Heads to add to their amp collection, deeming them essential for recording, but you don’t have to! Yellow mode is the reincarnation of the fabled Mark IIC+ Lead mode. Its blend of bold punch & evenly stacked liquid harmonics produces a lead voice that transforms any player who spends enough time to let it, into a virtuoso of feeling, soul & statement. It growls with ferocity in lows, staying tight & urgent. A thonk & chirp is experienced traveling through the mids. Then suddenly, as if someone redialed for the highs, an explosive, yet liquid, top end comes ripping out as you squeeze every luscious note from the treble strings. Sound almost sexual? Primal? Well many a IIC+ junkie will confess, broken hearts are often cured from a couple weeks rocking with one. Seriously, the blend of this mode is so amazing most players are finding new great sounds 2 & 3 years after their 1st ear to ear grin.

While Yellow mode excels at medium to high gain settings, because of these nicely stacked harmonics, don’t underestimate it for rootsier low gain sounds. Sure, as you can make high gain sounds chirp & squeal on command, low gain sounds possess the sting essential to tortured blues soloing. Yellow doesn’t get as saturated as Green in LEAD 2, making it the choice for skinnier, more cutting & clean blues lines. PRESENCE control works extremely well in Yellow mode, dialing in & out harmonic content of a given preset. At low PRESENCE & TREBLE settings, the sound is more horn or voice like. With higher settings of Presence & possibly Treble, the character becomes much more searing & harmonic”
tips: “LD2 Yellow is my absolute favorite. It’s the IIC+ mode. It has Pull Shift & Pull Bright enabled by default. I find this model easier to dial in than the IIC+ models & it sounds awesome.” – yek

Unique gain structure doesn’t use high #s of cascading gain stages compressing life out of tone, nor use any solid state clipping. Amp OD generated by running each gain to absolute extreme, just keeping them this side of instability. Helps preserve dynamic range, noise to minimum, emphasize harmonic overtones of each note, not sounding bright/harsh”
Concept was produce amp that reproduces my fav mod rock amp tones & modern higher gain tones without mush/noise

“In Triptik, initial bass cut happens after 1st gain stage, incrementally brought back in through next stages, while also controlling & manipulating high & mid bands too. There’s several filters at various points in gain stages to manipulate these other bands. 1 band’s always relative to other 2. In other words, wanting more bass, don’t necessarily have to increase that, can attenuate other 2 bands to create same effect. Keeping bass out of earlier stages allows each stage to be set up for more gain, for more gain from less stages, keeps S/N ratio down & dynamic range up. Feedback loop in power amp is freq dependent & allows more mid-highs to pass back to phase inverter on inverted input out-of-phase with normal input, which flattens response & lowers power amp gain (closed loop gain) much more for just those 2 bands. Bass band not attenuated near as much so amplified at level closer to open loop gain of power amp.” – Alan Phillips

tips: Cliff’s Tech Note: “A real Trainwreck Express is a fizzy, spitty amp. Some people like this, same people who like fuzz pedals & that quasi-half-wave rectified sound. Personally, I like more clarity. Reason Express is like this is primarily due to the last triode stage before the phase inverter (PI). This stage is biased very cold & drives the PI very hard due to lack of any limiting resistor (grid stopper) between triode & PI. Lack of a grid stopper resistor & large coupling capacitor create significant bias excursion (blocking distortion). Appears designer attempted minimizing bias excursion by biasing the triode cold, which limits positive excursion & therefore limits PI grid conduction. Despite the cold bias point, PI grid is still heavily overdriven, resulting in massive blocking distortion. AxeFx allows you to reduce amount of block distortion via PI Bias Excursion parameter. Simply turn it down & spittiness goes away, can also rebias the triode via Preamp Bias parameter. Values closer to 0 result in a more symmetric waveform.” & “Turn PI Bias Excursion to 0. Set Preamp Bias to -0.15 or so”

As no Dumbles are identical, stands to reason a person’s interpretation of ideal Dumble voicing won’t agree with another’s. Since V1 is runs clean, can get more gain increasing Input Trim, similar effect as increasing trimmer”

“Signal divider, correctly called voltage divider, calculated by taking resistance to ground divided by sum of resistances. Here, 26.7/317=0.084, close to values given (0.078). Our model uses local feedback on V1B (~2-3dB less gain), accounts for voltage divider’s affect on AC load-line. Dumble stages usually has AC load-line different from DC load-line due to load resistance’s significance in relation to plate resistor. As V1A & V1B run clean (linear), Input Trim accomplishes same thing as raising trimmer into drive stages, as linear system is commutative (see any intro Signals & Systems text for linear system properties). Commutative property is where AxB=BxA, so doesn’t matter if gain is before or after linear stages”

“Blackface Fender Tremolux was produced from 1963-66 & had 1 circuit model, blackface Tremolux AA763. In terms of power & clean headroom it’s the smallest of all Fender piggy back amps

Blackface Tremolux & Bandmaster (AB763) are almost identical amps, but Tremolux is sized for smaller events & gigs. The Tremolux had tube rectifier, while blackface Bandmaster had diode. Both amps had tremolo but no reverb. Tremolux speaker cab was 2×10” & not 2×12”. Tremolux had smaller transformers (power & output) than Bassman & Bandmaster. All this adds up to an amp with less volume, less clean headroom & more sag/compression, a more forgiving tone. It feels very much like a blackface Bandmaster, normal channel of Vibrolux Reverb & Pro Reverb or normal channel of earliest blackface Bassman (AA864). Sound is nice & clean & tone remains relatively clean when one turns volume knob. One doesn’t reach sweet spot as early as with Reverb-amps with additional gain stage in preamp section. Tremolux uses only 1 12ax7 tube in preamp section in both channels before signal enters phase inverter. Tremolux is appreciated for its simple & basic circuit. A less complicated circuit means fewer things that can go wrong, less component drift issues, easier to service & has less potential for noise problems. Tremolux is rarer vs other blackface piggy back amps, since it was produced over a shorter period of time. It was discontinued in 1966. 2×10” closed cabinet that came with Tremolux is practically sized & performs well on most stages. Oxfords or CTS speakers were delivered with these cabs in blackface years. A 2×10” cab is easier to carry around vs 2×12” cab & with the right (wrong) speakers, can get almost as loud as the 12s just with less spread, lower bass & mids. Jumping channels in AA763 Tremolux can give a wider spectrum of tones than by using just 1 channel. You may for example use normal channel to deliver bass tones & vibrato channel for sparkling clean sound with bright switch on & 0 bass. This gives you a full & meaty tone you won’t get using just 1 channel. Tremolux came without a mid pot”
Was Fender’s 1st amp with built-in tremolo (vibrato). Has been described as larger version of Fender’s Tweed Deluxe

If an emulation sounds darker or more midrangey than real amp, try turning down MV. If it’s a good emulation, should find a point (~1-2) you can hear the power amp start to saturate. “This mode is made for shred. In fact, it may be better named LEAD 2 Shred. It’s much more aggressive in top end vs its’ yellow counterpart, boasting much enhanced upper harmonics. Though it shares almost identical basic architecture, additional parts switch in with Red that give this once balanced, well behaved mode a downright ugly attitude. Harmonics are boosted & a bit of lower treble is dipped to give this Red a sizzling edge unique to this mode only. The harmonic edge not only benefits high notes, it does wonders for the grinding “Z’s” needed for bodacious low end crunch. This enhances the growl on the low strings & adds cut/sizzle to higher strings. The freqs enhanced by this circuit are slightly higher than those found in conventional power section PRESENCE controls. They’re also higher, more rebellious & defined than those adjusted by the action of TriAxis’ PRESENCE. These highs have that out-of-control-vibe to them, that falling-apart-yet-loosely-held-together quality that’s often associated with modded early British heads, using Euro-style EL34 power tubes for their ponies. This elusive sound affects string feel & players accustomed to such sounds have difficulty feeling at home on an amp that doesn’t deliver these loose highs.”

“...Pre-tone-control gain circuits. This means boosting gain by progressively slamming the 12AX7 tubes occurs before the tone controls. This method of squeezing gain through the tone controls tends to lend itself to a larger, yet slightly less focused, sound. Many rely on this looser, more spread out sound to be able to get emotional with their soloing style. This circuit also delivers large amounts of bass very well. As opposed to a “rear-end” style circuit, this circuit type lets you pump larger quantities of bass through the tone controls, without increased flub/cloudiness. Players wanting extremely high gain metal or hard rock sounds find LEAD 1 much more suited to the maxed out gain regions needed to produce over the top, believable crunch & grind.
See 315 USA Pre Clean for more amp info, tips & settings
tips: We especially recommend Lead1 Red for this application. This aggressive mode shares much of the circuitry with both Lead 1 Green & Yellow, then adds extra focus & punch in the upper mids. This mid-forward voicing lends a more urgent, tight character to the mix, perfect for showcasing Lead 1’s heavier side. Because of this added midrange, the Red mode slices through a mix in the sonic region where rock snare lives, especially great for crunch rhythm in classic or modern gain realms. Another attribute of this EQ’ing is that higher settings of Bass remain tighter & track better at higher gain settings vs the other Lead 1 modes. This additional bump in the mid freqs also allows more Treble to be dialed in, which increases gain without sounding thin. Try setting GAIN 8.0, BASS 6.5, TREBLE 7.0 & LEAD 1 DRIVE 6.0 to audition this”

[Response to complaints about “fizzy” Plexis] “What you’re hearing is output transformer high freq resonance. Old Plexis didn’t do this, as they had good transformers. New transformers are crappy & resonate at cutoff freq, as they’re underdamped, causing raspy, fizzy texture to distortion. Transformer resonance is adjustable, but parameter isn’t exposed to user. When you turn it up, you get that same squishy rasp that you’re hearing. For Plexis, I have damping set to flat, with no resonance, since that’s how our vintage Plexis measure. 50W is little underdamped, but people complain about raspy high freqs so I erred on safe side.”
“Way Plexi is supposed to sound, due to cathode follower. Raspiness helps cut through mix. I own 3, they’re fizzy.”
“Don’t be afraid to turn bass 100% down or treble 100% up, just like actual amp. Ex: on Normal channel of Plexi, most people turn bass way down, otherwise it’s too flubby.”

“Modding Marshalls for higher gain, sometimes modder decrease input freq response to reduce noise/fizz. To replicate: lower input EQ’s high-cut freq, or use high-shelf filter (little more subtle). “Distortion from power amp, tone controls don’t do much”

Why’s Plexi become such a popular amp? “1st/most important perhaps is sense of dynamics & rich harmonics. No large-production amp created before/since early Marshall plexis have been able to capture feel of player through varying degrees of dynamics/color from (mostly) EL34-based tube circuits of these Marshalls. Call it a lucky accident with Marshall, but they created amps that really responded well to guitars played through them. Amps deliver wide palette of distortion color, rich, full, powerful & timeless in tone. Takes some time to really get used to playing basic amp, like a Marshall plexi. No multi channels, reverb or effects & no MV controls. Turn up amp, play hard & get tone fullness & smooth distortion. Back off playing, amp will respond/move to lighter shades of OD. Roll down guitar volume a touch & get warmed up clean sound. There’s nothing like ability to feel set of power & preamp tubes overdriving together musically.”–Legendary Tones

Like original Plexi, 1959SLP doesn’t have a Master, so keep Master control in amp model cranked. Without a MV control, Plexi amps rely on power amp distortion. To achieve a nice overdriven rock tone, you need to turn up a Plexi a lot. This makes it a very loud amp in real life

notes: ‘65 blackface AB763, Normal channel
Fender Deluxe Reverb, aka “DR”, isn’t same as Fender Deluxe with added reverb. It is, kinda, but amp sounds different, more scooped

“The Deluxe Reverb 1x12” has for decades been one of the most popular amps among all Fender amps & its popularity is still growing as the demand for low wattage tube amps increases. The combination of size, weight & performance makes the Deluxe Reverb a true road warrior on gigs & practice. Both the Deluxe Reverb (DR) & Princeton Reverb (PR) “survived” the CBS silverface periods with minor changes. Many people consider the silverface amps just as sonically good as the blackface models. Being almost a blackface amp with a new faceplate (wrong for collectors), the silverface models became popular value-for-the-money amps. Collectors hunt the blackface models & players hunt the silverface for its quality & price. DR is a small/medium-sized amp with an ability to deliver both sparkling clean tones & low wattage breakup at 22W with 6V6 tubes & relatively small transformers (power & output). It has found its way in to more recording studios, clubs & bars than any other Fender amp. It has met many players’ expectations. It is just powerful enough to cut through in practice in a band with a drummer and, unlike some bigger amps, it will reach its sweet spot at a reasonable volume. It has the typical blackface 60s sparkle with a scooped clean sound just like the bigger Fender brothers, just with more smooth breakup, sag & compression”

“An equally fine choice for a versatile small club amp is the Vibrolux Reverb’s little brother, the Blackface Deluxe Reverb (1964 through 1967). It is rated at just 24 watt or so (with two 6V6 power tubes), but the overall circuitry in the amp is virtually the same as the Vibrolux Reverb. It has two channels, but I only use the second channel, again, due to the extra stage of gain. It drives a single 12” speaker. Most of the Deluxe Reverbs that Fender built have a very inefficient Oxford 12” in them. The first thing you should do to make this amp really worthy is to install a much larger ceramic magnet speaker. A better 12” is essential to having a Deluxe sound as good as it possibly can (and that is very good indeed.) The Deluxe Reverb will not have as much bottom as a Vibrolux Reverb, due to its smaller power tubes, but anyone who’s heard a Deluxe Reverb set at about “6” for leads knows how sweet the 6V6 power tubes sound. Again, you need to run this amp at “6” or above in terms of volume to really bring out the classic overdriven Fender tone. I find that setting my guitar’s volume knob on “10” for leads works wonderfully, then when I back it off to say “7” or so for rhythm, the amp naturally cleans up. That’s a neat trick to use. If you are hesitant to change your original speaker, consider acquiring a second speaker cabinet for your new & improved speaker. But remember, amps are tone machines, not museum pieces, so if you are torn between swapping out the speaker, keep in mind that you can always store it away & reinstall it if you decide to sell the amp later. I have an extension cabinet with a 15” Electrovoice SRO speaker in it & I sometimes run my own Deluxe Reverb through that setup. It dramatically improves the tone—huge fat bottom, low mids & much more overall volume.” – ToneQuest

“22-watt ’65 Deluxe Reverb amp is for rock, country or blues players who want a moderately powered amp they can crank up at the gig or in the studio. The full, snappy guitar tones heard on many famous recordings from Memphis to Abbey Road were made using the Deluxe amp. Features include dual 6V6 Groove Tubes output tubes, one 5AR4 rectifier tube, four 12AX7 preamp tubes, two 12AT7 tubes, one 12” 8-ohm Jensen C-12K speaker, dual channels (normal & vibrato), tube-driven Fender reverb, tube vibrato, two button footswitch for reverb & vibrato on-off, black textured vinyl covering & silver grille cloth.”

Deluxe Reverb has Normal & Vibrato channels, both modeled because of different characteristics. Most people use Vibrato channel but Normal channel is pretty cool too, especially for single note runs & jazzy tunes.
“Values for Deluxe Reverb are based on measurements of actual 65 Deluxe Reverb, not some hypothetical values on some spec sheet.”

“We got our reference Deluxe Reverb out of storage today, hooked it up & measured & compared. Gain measures spot-on & A/B testing sounds identical. With a Suhr Modern guitar with stock pickups both the amp & the model were starting to break up around 3 (which equals 2.2 on the Axe-Fx since the knobs start at zero not one). A Deluxe Reverb breaks up easily since it has 6V6 power tubes. The preamp is virtually identical to a Twin Reverb but 6V6s break up earlier than 6L6s. For a given voltage into the power amp a 6V6 has about 70% of the headroom compared to a 6L6.”
tips: Chimey tone, breaks up nicely when pushed

(make Twin cleaner) “Reduce MV (or MV Trim). Biggest reason Silverface Twins were cleaner is PI had less gain. Reducing MV or MV Trim will simulate lower gain.”

(Original Double Verb model) “Twin Reverb model’s based on breaks up easy. Extremely accurate, a Blackface Twin, breaks up easy vs later ones. As with all models, modeled on Hi input. Don’t want break up as easy? Input Trim 0.5 simulates Low input, cut Input Drive & MV if needed. Can turn Bright Switch off. Those wanting squeaky clean often turn Bright Switch off, but you’d be surprised Twin isn’t nearly as clean as thought, just so damn loud you get sensation it’s clean, as light touch on strings creates lotta volume”

“Dual Showman with AB763 circuit has 1 less gain stage than Twin Reverb, it has less gain. There’s 2 gain stages. Vibrato channel of AB763 Twin Reverb has 3 gain stages. AA769 Dual Showman Reverb Vibrato channel has similar gain, has 3 gain stages. AB763 Dual Showman isn’t same circuit as AB763 Twin Reverb”

Twin Reverb may be Fender’s most popular amp. It’s big, loud, takes pedals well & ultra clean. Getting amp into OD requires volume level hardly anyone can handle, unless modded. Twin handles humbuckers well, which isn’t the case with all Fenders

“If aliens came to earth & wanted to hear an American guitar sound, I’d play him my Twin with set of Jensens. This was stated by a happy Twin Reverb owner on Harmonycentral.com. It could have been our own words. The Twin Reverb is the king of Fender blackface amps. Having two pairs of 6L6, the popular & traditional two-channel AB763 circuit design, a diode rectifier & enormous transformers (power & output), it offers tons of clean headroom & volume for unmiked gigs & really big stages. Where the other Fender amps break up at around 4 on the volume knob, the Twin stays clean up to almost 6 & will hold up against heavy drummers & bass players with clean notes sharp as a knife edge. This is exactly what the amp is made for, being played unmiked in a gospel band in a 300-seat church every Sunday. It is designed not break up like the other Fender amps. You need to have your expectations set correctly to be able to appreciate the evil Twin. Warning nr 1) The big transformers & speakers makes this amp weigh around 40kgs, a burden too big for many gigging players who cannot (yet) afford a crew of roadies. Warning nr 2) Volume & clean headroom. If you want tube amp breakup & smoking tones with no pedals you will experience many fights with your band mates & club owners. Just as the other Fender amps the Twin needs to operate in its sweet spot up to sound sweet. After carrying a Twin Reverb on to the stage, the least you should deserve is to crank the bastard. Sadly, we are seldom offered the opportunity to turn the volume above 3 on a Twin Reverb. Instead we have played many nights with a thin & unpleasant tone, even worse with a sparkling, clean sounding strat.” – Fenderguru.com

“AB763 Super Reverb’s a very popular Fender due to huge tone, robustness & pure tone. Blackfaces have more growl & distorted, cranked tone. Big sounding amp with potential for being very loud & bassy, given the right (wrong) speakers. Nature of 4×10” speaker config is a directional tone with screaming treble right forwards & backwards & unfortunately little spread. Lot of deep bass produced by the big cab, while mids are fairly low, a scooped tone. Many players are stupid & increase volume to compensate for lack of spread & mids, introduces even more bass & sharp treble. Playing a Super Reverb isn’t supposed to be easy, despite difficulty of this amp, there’s sometimes gigs where amp won’t hurt anyone in 3 meter radius. Turn the volume beyond 4, where amp comes alive. We remember these occasions as our happiest musical moments. Notes bounce off our strings & we’re musically & physically connected with the amp just using pick attack & guitar volume to roll back & switch from rhythm & solo. Maybe a transparent boost pedal to take us to David Gilmour land, with sustain, harmonics & creamy tone. Can physically feel dynamic response from 1 of the best vintage Fender amps, only if you tame the beast
The original modeled amp has been modded for more drive

“Super Reverb commonly used by blues guitarists for its loud, warm tube distortion through its 4 10” speakers. Also known for a scooped mids tonality, so there’s less midrange & emphasis of sparkly treble & full, round bass freqs”

Fender sold these amps with several speakers. 1st AA763 models in ‘64-65 had Jensen C10r. Then there were CTS ceramics & alnicos, as well as Oxford 10L6 in blackface AB763 amps. In silverface amps, Fender continued with Oxford & CTS, also used Utah, Rola & Eminence. This is a reason why 2 Super Reverbs can sound very different. In our opinion, Super Reverbs with Jensen & CTS are valuable, as both collectors & players’ amps today. These speakers perform very well & one doesn’t need to upgrade to modern, efficient speakers, like many other vintage speakers. CTS alnicos are also very popular speakers, even if they’re little efficient. During the years, Alnico magnets get weaker too. CTS Alnico require you to increase volume a lot & you’ll see players that dial in their amps at 6-7 on volume knob. With ceramic speakers, this is enormously loud. With vintage Alnico speakers, you’ll get more breakup from amp due to their low efficiency. On other hand, CTS ceramics are known for their power, efficiency & full low end. They also have lots of sparkle & treble & very good speakers in our opinion”

“AC30’s have poorly designed cathode follower. Bias point’s wrong & crushes 1 signal side considerably. IMO either cath. resistor should be 100K or 200K plate resistor of previous stage. Clipping is extremely asymmetric, too much IMO. Little asymmetry is good/warms things up, too much has excessive even harmonics, makes things fuzzy/indistinct. Clipping’s so asymmetric, almost half-wave rectifier

Can tweak by adjusting Preamp Bias point &/or lower Cathode Follower Compress, or lower Harmonics value, reduces asymmetric distortion, but ODs phase inverter, causes blocking distortion via excess bias excursion

Also try increasing Grid Clipping, adds some headroom. Start via Bias point. AC30 are sensitive to tube type & part tolerances, tiny change make big difference. Default bias point is based on Mullard ECC83 tubes. I prefer AC-20, it doesn’t have cathode follower & doesn’t suffer from these problems. Cathode follower in AC30 doesn’t do all that much. Normally, use cathode follower to pre-set a low-impedance source to tone stack, but in AC30 doesn’t have a great load anyways.”

“A deceptively simple amp, capable of early 60s British tones & more. EF86 tube help make range of tones from cleanest of EL84 chime to ferocious high gain growl. Power level control allows dialing in right volume, not sacrificing tone like some MV do. AC20 was created to solve modern guitar player amp issues, ability to stay true to vintage tonality, equally at home, in studio, or gigs. Seen on stages of Jeff Tweedy, Tim McGraw, The Band Perry & Toshi Yanagi (Jimmy Kimmel). Plug in & notice familiar chime/compression of Class A EL84 driven output. Quoting Keith Armstrong (Chief Engineer at Mix LA) “It’s impossible to get a bad sound out of this amp!” AC20 Deluxe uses 3 separate switches to give all the original early 60’s EL84 tonalities, Normal, Brilliant & EF86. “The world’s greatest rock amp is a Marshall “Plexi”

(Reply to top end squish when digging in) ”What you hear is output transformer high freq resonance. Old Plexis didn’t do it, they had good transformers. New ones are crappy & resonate at cutoff freq, since they’re underdamped, it causes raspy, fizzy texture to distortion. Transformer resonance adjustable but parameter isn’t exposed to FAS users. When you turn it up you get that same squishy rasp you’re hearing. For Plexis I have damping set flat with no resonance, as that’s how our vintage Plexis measure. Our 50W is little underdamped but people complain about raspy highs so I erred on safe side” - Cliff
(Reply to BMT knobs doing little to tone) “All distortion comes from power amp, so tone controls don’t do much”

So why’s Plexi become so popular amp? “1st n maybe most important is sense of dynamics/rich harmonics. No large-production amp created before/after early Plexi series has captured feel of a player through varied degrees of dynamics & coloration from (mostly) EL34 tube circuits. Call it a lucky accident with Marshall, but they were able to create amplifiers that really responded well to guitars played through them. Wide palette of distortion color that’s rich, full, powerful & timeless in tone is what these amps deliver. Takes some time to really get used to playing a basic amp like a plexi. No multi channels, reverb, effects & no master volume. Turn up the amp & play. Play hard & amp rewards you with fullness of tone & smooth distortion. Back off playing, amp will respond & move into lighter shades of OD. Roll down guitar volume some for warm clean sound. There’s nothing like feeling a set of power/preamp tubes ODing together musically” -
Plexis are raw, unrefined, honest & touch sensitive. Hit a power chord & feel explosion of sound in your face/body
Numerous guitar heroes played some kind of Plexi: Pete Townsend, Jimi Hendrix, Jimmy Page, Angus Young, Yngwie Malmsteen, Jeff Beck & of course Eddie Van Halen
Some people complain that a Plexi sounds fizzy. “It’s the way a Plexi’s supposed to sound, due to cathode follower. That raspiness helps it cut through a mix. I own 3, all fizzy”

Many Plexi players use patch cables to jumper inputs: 2nd input of channel 1 goes to 1st input of channel 2 for benefit of both channels at once & 2 Drive controls. Set at same position, or keep Normal Drive lower vs Treble Drive

“Don’t be afraid to turn bass low/treble high, like real amp”

“1 of 1st mods people make to real Plexi Marshalls is clip the bright cap, which varied over years, supposedly depended on what was lying around in shop. Model defaults to bright cap in circuit. “VARIAC (“Variable A/C”) is a unit that changes voltage coming out the wall to a lower amount, like a light dimmer. When a VARIAC’s used in conjunction with SLP, can act loosely as Master Volume. notes: (OD channels) “It’s a crazy idea I know, but 2 channels are identical. Generally, logic & intuition would tell you rational thing to do if you got 4 channels is make them all different. That said, I’ve realized, particularly from playing live, once you get tone dialed in, you wish you could also get it a little bit louder, with slightly different EQ. I’ve found this the case more often than not & no one wants to walk around with 2 heads if they don’t have to, they’d much rather have 1 head with sounds in it. Hence, reason for OD1 & OD2 being the same. So working with Santiago, we made the 2 channels essentially the same as OD1 on original JVM410H, but then, at a click of a programmable button, the added Mid-Shift, you can make either, or both of them, be identical to original JVM OD2 channel too, in terms of EQ curve. So on JVM410HJS, you can dial in that big, full, organic “Get Your Buzz On” CF guitar tone. Or, you can activate that switch & there’s a bit of a scoop, which I found while still being a really fat tone, makes more room for Sammy’s vocal in overall shape of the sounds that make up Chickenfoot. But then, by the same token, I find that on my solo work, that space needs to be filled by my guitar, so I need extra midrange to do so. “5E3 Deluxe is desirable among players within many music styles. Tone is fat/rich with strong mids & decent bass response given relatively small cab size, approximately same size as Princeton Reverb. Construction of pine baffle & cab sounds tighter & more closed vs blackface open cabs, with possibility of more low end response given the right speaker. 12” speaker contributes to a full, warm tone & pure/simple tone stack of 5E3 Circuit delivers natural & uncolored tone of guitar

Known for its distorted & cranked tones, comes easily when volume/tone is above 12 o’clock. Early distortion partly by lack of negative feedback loop & 6V6 cathode bias design, which offers more sag & compression, less clean headroom than fixed bias (typically AB763 blackface amps & a few tweed amps). Besides fact that it distorts easily, what fascinates us most is golden tone secrets that exist within this amp. Experiment with tone knob & other channel’s volume knob (channel not plugged into), to find one of the most beautiful clean tones of all times & confirms Leo is a God of tone. Clean sound is not as loud, cold & terrifying as silverface/blackface era amps. They’ll require much more experience/effort to dial in sweet tones, but once you know how, you’re rewarded greatly. With 5E3 Deluxe, it’s easier to quickly dial in a nice clean tone, especially at low volume levels. Given early distortion & mellow clean sound, 5E3 Deluxe is great for single coil guitars, especially bright bridge pickup of Strat & Tele

Looking at the control panel, 5E3 Deluxe appears to be very simple. Few controls provide quick & small selection of tones. It’s practically impossible to not find a good tone with this amp. Just need to turn up volume & set tone. We believe the world would be a better place if the 5E3 Deluxe was the only amp around. All guitar players deserve to play this amp & learn how to create music with natural & transparent guitar tone. But amp isn’t really as simple as one might think. 2 interactive volume channels & mysterious, non-linear tone control provides a big spectrum of tones, everything from Fender clean to Marshall grit. Many players find the 2 volume controls confusing. We agree. What the heck was Leo & his engineers really thinking when they designed the 2 volume controls? When you plug into the normal channel any normal person, even a drummer, would expect the other channel’s setting isn’t affecting tone. But no. As you gradually turn the other volume knob, both tone & volume changes, drastically at very end between 10 & 12 where you’d expect nuthin more to come. It works likewise the other way around if you play the bright channel. Even more confusing is the tone control. You might expect a treble or mid control. Nope, tone control affects volume, gain, EQ/tone, everything & worse, it doesn’t behave consequently at different volume levels of 2 channels. In total you have 4 inputs to choose from, 2 volume knobs & a tone knob that you can spend years trying to figure out”
