Other 2 channels contain modes that work better for soft clip, medium crunch & high gain rhythm work. There’s a tight, skinny CLEAN, a warm, rich FAT clean sound with added lower fundamental & a higher gain pushed version of this architecture found in TWEED. BOLD voicing switch adds punch & cut starting in high mids to help stand out in a dense mix & more headroom

POWER: MULTI-WATT: Determines amount (wattage) & type (configuration) of power each preamp Channel will be coupled with to create a classic sound. Any amp’s sound is 50% preamp & 50% power, so this switch is responsible for a large part of a Channel’s personality & feel. Choices repeat for all 3 Channels & they’re 90W, 45, & 10W. Just select power wanted for each Channel, keep in mind the greatest headroom, focus & authority will always be found in 90w position

Since ‘81, Simul-Class Power has been the heart & soul of the MARK Series amps, imparting its sweet, musical character onto any sound. Cleans that shimmer with transparent layers of sweet delicate highs, bottom end breathes a warm fundamental under a bed of rich low mid ambience. Never harsh, always fat, Simul lead tone is quintessential single-note solo sound best described with a human trait vocal.
Patented way of wiring an output section combines 2 power tube pairs with different bias settings & operating parameters, arriving at a blend showing the best attributes of both.

In simplified terms, Simul-Class output comprises 2 dissimilar pairs of power tubes operating simultaneously. 1 pair operates more toward Class A for tone, other pair runs traditional Class AB to provide extra horsepower needed for clean headroom. Since 1980, Simul-Class has evolved & improved, providing more power, while still eliminating any trace of harshness.

In the MkII-C+, Class A pair was permanently wired in Triode configuration & in MkV, it can still be achieved (Channel 3 only). By reducing the tubes’ power sensitivity, Triode wiring pushes the pair even further into Class A. This results in more dynamic compression & greater harmonic spread for the ultimate single-note fluid sustain but reduces clean headroom substantially.

90w position is full Simul-Class mode with all 4 6L6s combining the 2 different bias settings to deliver max power & headroom. It’s substantially sweeter/warmer & a little more scooped vs a standard 100w amp, yet has plenty of punch & authority without harshness.

45w turns off outer pair of 6L6s, so only middle 2 are running, the ones with lowered bias so, while they’re still Class AB, their Class A region is extended. In Channel 3, they can be switched to run in Triode configuration which cuts clean headroom roughly in half.

Combining these 2 opposite styles of wiring in 1 amp gives you the best of vintage & modern amp styles. Headroom & power are there when you need it, but there is always a naturally pleasing & musically curvaceous quality to the sound that’s magic to your ears & hands. Simul feels great & is inspiring to play!

10w reconfigures the whole set of 6L6s so that 2 nearest the 5U4 run pure Class A, single-ended, no longer push-pull, the ultimate low wattage output circuit that duplicates the essence of the best really old vintage circuits. Here, the 2nd harmonic (octave above note played) is NOT canceled out (as it is in push-pull circuits) & provides a magical halo surrounding notes. Onset of clip is so gradual, it’s hard to pin down transition from clean to overdriven.

BIAS SELECT switch allows you to run EL34 power tubes in place of the stock compliment of 6L6’s. EL34-style tubes produce a brighter, skinnier sound that will clip with a whole different harmonic content that can be nice, especially for recording where you may not need the Channel switching performance of all 3 Channels & can dedicate the amp to a specific sound. 6L6’s will most likely perform better for wide range of sounds & sound fatter/richer on most all sounds & have the most clean headroom.

GAIN & TREBLE Controls are the most powerful tone shaping controls & should be used with taste. They determine much about the attack characteristic & overall personality of the sound in all Modes. Many of the great sounds in all Channels will find these 2 Controls in their middle ranges. Avoid setting TREBLE high (above 2:00) when GAIN is set high, as it has the tendency for a slightly microphonic tube to ring or squeal.

When using high GAIN settings, try EQ for adding extra top end, as it comes later in signal chain & less stressful on the preamp tubes. Remember, MkV is a high performance amp in every sense. Just like a highly tuned car, don’t need to drive it wide open to have fun. You can get amazing performance in the middle ranges of all controls.

PRESENCE is very powerful at shaping voicing of high gain sounds in Channels 3 (& even TWEED in Channel 1). Set low, it fattens & compresses the sound, for a more voice-like focused note. Higher settings “open up” the sound & allow the full spectrum of harmonics to flow through. Use to fine tune your lead sounds after you’ve dialed the rest of the preamp controls to your liking

Beware of setting BASS too high in Channels 3, especially when GAIN is set high. Too much BASS produces flubby, indistinct attack. In Mk1 Mode of Channel 2 it’s perfectly respectable & even recommended to run BASS control extremely low (8:30) or even off when GAIN is set high (above 1:30). Modes in Channel 3 can stand some more BASS, but watch it there as well. A basic rule might be this, as GAIN goes up, BASS should come down.

NORMAL switch mode sounds more round, rich & warm & is a pure solo voice. BRIGHT lifts the veil, allowing a whole spectrum of higher harmonics to soar through unimpeded, for that classic Boogie stacked harmonic spread.
TRIODE/PENTODE switch affects Channel 3 wiring of power tubes & sound. TRIODE softens attack & makes strings feel more liquid. PENTODE tightens attack, adds midrange punch & headroom

Speaker Impedance has a large sonic effect on the sounds as the power section is switched between its 3 different Modes. We prefer matching 8ohm speaker load connected to 8ohm SPEAKER OUTPUT for the most balanced sound & overall performance in all 3 Channels. However, Simul-Class Output Section is a mysterious animal & produces some interesting & musical results when different loads are applied. One favorite is connecting the 8ohm speaker load to the 4ohm SPEAKER OUTPUT when using the 45w (Half Power) setting. Feel free to experiment with different load combos. You may discover an impedance scenario that, though is a technical mismatch, produces a unique response that fits your needs.

Channel 1: Lowest gain of 3 Channels. 2 Modes CLEAN & FAT are structured for clean sounds. These 2 modes are well described by their names, CLEAN is sweet, sparkling low gain beauty & FAT adds big low end & breathiness to sound. These 2 have the greatest headroom & most dynamic range & sensitivity. They’re the least compressed & retain the fastest attack characteristic.

Lowest gain of 3 Channels & will cover all your clean rhythm & solo styles & slightly driven chording sound needs. As with Modes in each Channel, we start with slimmed down (skinnier), tighter voice of CLEAN & move up the girth scale to FAT & finally to slightly higher mid-gain of TWEED.

CLEAN is derived from a blend of Mk series clean sounds taken from MkIV & perfect for rhythm comping in ensemble environments, where guitar has to fit in a defined spot of a more complex mix. It’s also extremely accurate in the time domain & has a balanced blend of tight low end to sparkling, immediacy of the top end. Mode also clips great in 45 & 10w power modes with its’ well balanced, more stripped nature.

FAT stands in sharp contrast to this, with big breathy bottom that extends down into the sub-low region & adds air to the entire spectrum as the top end gets more bubbly & spacial. This sound pays tribute to the best blackface inspired sounds & circuit relies heavily on architecture from Input 2 of the original MkI & MkV CLEAN Mode. FAT excels at big, featured chording parts & single note clean soloing & a great choice for clipped sounds (with BASS control set low) in 45 or 10w power mode.

TWEED adds a boost in the mids & rolls back some top end, to create a sound that punches through a mix with mid authority & clips with a more rounded vocal quality. It works great for lower gain crunch rhythm parts & can add a healthy dose of top end cut with PRESENCE, as there’s less upper harmonics to get hashy/buzzy

CHANNEL 1 VOICE SWITCH (NORMAL/BOLD): Offers 2 choices in voicing mids & upper mids/lower treble region. NORMAL has a balanced smooth response that shines for both shimmering sweet clean sounds & creamy soft-clip tones as modes are driven harder with the GAIN control. No particular freqs stick out in this position, which creates a perfect base for rhythm work & makes NORMAL respond very well to further embellishment with the EQ

BOLD punches through with a pronounced bump in these mid & upper mid/low treble freqs to cut through a dense mix & be heard. It gives the impression of increased power & headroom, as cleans sounds fly out the speakers with immediacy & authority. Likewise, OD sounds, especially in TWEED, take the added attack & turn it into stinging aggression. Be sure to work with TREBLE, MID & PRESENCE in BOLD to fine tune these regions & optimize both the sound & feel.

CLEAN is derived from classic Mk circuits & puts emphasis on tight, focused clean rhythm & articulate single note playing. This mode has the greatest clean headroom of any mode in the amp & though it can be pushed to clip at extreme settings (4:00-5:30), it’ll remain tighter & somewhat stiffer than FAT when used for this. The good side of this stiffness is the BASS control can occasionally be set higher vs going for clipped sounds in FAT, as the overall personality of CLEAN is stripped of sub-low freqs that can be challenging when looking for aggressive threshold rhythm sounds.

CLEAN works very well for aggro & brash clipped chording sounds, especially when Power Select is set to 45w & PRESENCE is a bit high (1:00-2:30). Try this vibe for Punk or super fast Rock rhythm styles & need aggressive almost-clean sounds that start & stop instantaneously.

CLEAN shines for chording & arpeggiated work with its crystalline top end sparkle & high harmonic openness. Low end is tucked up higher so it adds breath & warmth, but doesn’t go too low, so won’t get too big/sluggish & get in the way if a groove calls for precise rhythmic note durations. Great for skanky Funk rhythm/burning Country pickin.

Midrange freqs are a bit higher in freq vs FAT mode, enabling a percussive attack that stays tight & has max impact in a range that cuts & protects its territory in a complex mix. Playing with these higher mids can be a powerful way to shape the CLEAN mode, as the role they play either brings sound forward, even in the time domain, making it seem faster, or lends a recessive, more relaxed quality to the sound, making it seem slower. Experiment with BASS & MID & learn to tune the sound’s attack, width & girth in CLEAN to match style & tempos you play most.

Some Modes work better than others with the EQ & respond better to radical shaping power with a more harmonious demeanor. Generally speaking, Modes with less low end tend to work better & are usually the ones that have created classic sounds with EQ in place. CLEAN in Channel 1 & all Modes in Channel 3 (with MkIIC+ being most friendly) tend to be best for positive EQ reinforcement.

GAIN: By far the most powerful control in the MkV & settings determine the style & personality of all 3 Modes in each channel. It meters the gain in different tube stages depending on Channel & Mode & sets Input Stage headroom, which determines whether sound is clean or overdriven. It also acts as subtle Tone control as tube stages’ gain is increased/decreased & imparts its own “color” on the sound.

In all Channels, there’s 3 regions of GAIN, a low gain zone from 9:00-11:30, a warmer, more saturated zone from 12:00-2:00 & a higher gain zone from 2:30-5:30. Each zone can be used for many different applications & all can be used for both chording & single note solo work. As GAIN is swept throughout its range, it imparts different textures & tonal character.

Generally speaking, lower end (9:30-11:30) in all Channels/Modes produces a brighter, more open character & more dynamic content available. This region’s great for clean, sparkling chording in Channel 1, where max headroom is available, top end harmonics are bubbly & attack is lightning fast. Channel 3 also responds well in this lower region & similar chording/solo sounds await you here. The same Modes can sound so vintage-approved & agile when set low, can be ferocious high gain Modes when things get pushed.

Middle region of GAIN (12:00-2:00) is where the most balanced sounds live & delivers warm, full sound, detailed attack & good dynamics & Tone controls still have a powerful effect on signal. Channel 1 CLEAN & FAT Modes deliver great chording response, sound richer & have more body here. Depending on pickup style & strength, watch for clipping when nearing the crossover point, gain-wise. Channel 3 Modes offer their greatest flexibility, focus & detail in this middle zone. As these sounds are all higher gain vs their Channel 1 & 2 counterparts, the best dynamic response & attack character is in this window. Approaching 2:00, there will be plenty of saturation to keep chords grinding & single notes hanging, but not too much to start compressing the life out of the sound. If you not getting great gain sound results in this region for Channel 2 or 3, try pickups with a bit hotter output.

The highest region of GAIN (2:30-5:30) is all about saturation. Up here the signal gets much fatter in the low end & top end begins to recede for a round, compressed sound. Dynamics become slower with lower peaks & produces a more legato, creamier feel. In Channel 1, high end of GAIN produces some great “clipped clean” sounds as the Input stage gives up & starts to saturate. These sounds are further enhanced by the 45 & 10w Power Modes & VARIAC POWER setting. Channel 3 is absolutely over the top when GAIN is ran this high. The more midrange-prominent character of these Modes allows you to still have good articulation here, even with amounts of saturation that’d turn most circuits to useless mush. The focus, articulation & tightly-glued gain that sticks to notes & tracks flawlessly is a sound that’s pure Boogie. Up here, notice the Tone controls have a diminished effect on the sound, as notes are so saturated & their character has been pre-determined by the way each Mode is voiced & how it reacts to this gain level.

MASTER: Determines overall output level, located at the very end of the preamp. Using it in combination with GAIN, any amount of preamp signal strength, gain can be achieved at any playing volume. 1st get sound desired, then balance the volume levels with this control
For general applications & to get best performance out of all any mode, we recommend settings in 9:00-12:00 range with most settling in around 10:30 for average playing volumes.

Some like to run MASTER cranked & raise GAIN until they reach a desired sound, thinking this achieves the purest result. In theory, they believe this resembles removing the control altogether from the signal path & in a way it does. However most “vintage non-master” amps they’re seeking to emulate have discrete resistors in that place of the circuit, to adjust or “tune” the preamp output to the power section sensitivity. MASTER is nothing more than a variable resistor that offers an infinite range of settings possibilities & makes amp more versatile with no sonic penalty. If you prescribe to this old school approach, then by all means, use it this way, it won’t hurt. However you’ll be severely limiting potential sounds you can achieve by removing the limitless great sounding combinations of GAIN & MASTER settings.

PRESENCE: Adjusts high freqs above those of TREBLE, located in the power section, farther downstream in the signal path & not in the preamp. PRESENCE adjusts a specific zone of freqs in the negative feedback circuit of the power section for each individual Mode. The MkV incorporates substantial circuitry to achieve complex switching of parts needed to voice each Mode correctly & ensure an adjustable range on PRESENCE that’s sound-style appropriate & musically usable.

Can think of PRESENCE as a control that allows either clamping power amp down, compressing it & darkening things, or open it up & let the full spectrum of upper harmonics come blazing through. It also has a great deal to do with how dynamic the signal is & how a sound will cut through the mix in an ensemble environment.

At low settings (7:30-10:30) the sound will be warm & round with a more compressed feel & dynamic fluctuation will be limited. As it’s increased (11:00-2:30), top end starts to become more dominant & compression gives way to “cut” & dynamic peaks jump out with startling speed & accuracy. At the top end of control (2:30-5:30), a super aggressive blend of upper harmonics dominate the sound & this region can be somewhat dangerous if not applied in small measures. Higher notes will slice & dice even the bravest set of ears & we suggest using this region mostly in the studio for recording heavy crunch rhythm parts & even then, mostly on parts that feature lower strings. This region, especially when coupled with the inherent curve of many microphones typically used in P.A. (Sound reinforcement) applications can be truly punishing.

We suggest using lower to middle range of PRESENCE (9:00-12:30) for the best/most balanced sound in all Modes & venturing outside this only for specific uses, like needing more aggressive top-end point or darker, more compressed & wider sound.

Clean sounds in Channel 1 can generally benefit from a bit higher settings (10:30-12:30) than sounds in this, or any Channel, that has OD involved. Once saturation begins, the freqs carried in the control can make things edgy or brittle, even buzzy, real fast if not careful. Overdriven chording can tolerate higher settings (10:30-12:30) better than single note sounds, which usually want to roam the zone below 11:00 to stay round, focused & vocal.

High PRESENCE settings (2:30-5:30) can put extra stress on even borderline microphonic preamp tubes (ones susceptible to high pitched ringing & noise), causing them to begin ringing or show other signs of instability. Avoid these settings (especially in Combo amps, where added sympathetic & vibrational forces put even more stress on tubes) to ensure trouble free performance.

TREBLE: If VOLUME is the most powerful control in MkV, this comes in a close 2nd. It’s responsible for shaping the character of the amp. It can overpower the other Tone controls easily & therefore its setting is crucial to a rich & balanced sound in all Modes. In fact, TREBLE feeds the signal to MID & BASS controls & acts like a valve for their signal strength.

TREBLE set in its higher regions (2:00-5:30) it sends a smaller signal to those controls & they’re less active & the dominant character will be very bright, TREBLE-heavy freqs. Conversely, very low settings will produce sounds that may be a little BASS heavy & overly dark, as a very large amount of signal is shoveled toward MID & BASS. Setting with care & taste is critical for Tone control string to work in harmony.

In all Channels/Modes, the middle region of TREBLE has the best balance & creates sounds that are bright, but still rich & warm. We suggest you start with TREBLE at 12:00 & adjust up/down slightly until desired blend is achieved. Remember, you can use PRESENCE to add additional (& slightly higher) top end, with no penalty, in regards to effectiveness of other Tone controls, as it works in a part of the circuit that’s much farther down the line in the signal path.

Be aware of TREBLE when looking for clipped Blues sounds in Channel 1, with GAIN cranked. The additional gain added by running the TREBLE high (1:30-2:30) can help saturate enough to get some great pushed sounds. You’ll have to run BASS rather low (8:30-9:30) to keep things tight.

MID: Acts much more like a standard tone control & doesn’t have quite the massive global shaping power of VOLUME & TREBLE, yet its setting does impart strong character on the sound. It brings in & out a broad band of midrange freqs & a fair amount of higher “low treble” range freqs. These highs are lower than TREBLE or PRESENCE, but important for punch & cut of the amp in a mix.

For rhythm playing in CLEAN & FAT Modes of Channel 1, lower MID setting (7:30-10:00) scoops some of this midrange attack & makes bottom end breathe more. This range also makes things more resilient & create an easier to play, more elastic feel on the strings. Single coil guitars work very well here for the slinky, rubber band attack & bouncy bass character with Blues, R&B & Country clean styles.

Middle region (10:00-1:00) is where punch & attack begin to come on with more urgency & where mahogany guitars really like to see the MID set for adding cut & definition. Here, top end begins to creep into the mix of the MID controls’ spectrum & chording sounds start to chime & slash with a more forward & very present character.

From here on up (1:00-5:30) MID introduces aggressive sounds that are both full & quite forward as MID’s dominant freqs become more present. In this range, likely have to increase BASS to add back richness & warmth that gets overshadowed when MID is set high. If you like attack & urgency found in this range, all other controls (except maybe MASTER, which you may have to back down as sound gets more forward) may need to be set higher, to keep up with the MID dominant curve. This is fine, though there reaches a point of diminishing return, as headroom in the preamp gets eaten up by this tonal arms race & you begin to clip the preamp with the high signal from the Tone control string.

For gain sounds in Channel 3 Modes, a similar story unfolds as MID is increased. Lower settings (7:30-10:30) will produce wider sounding, more elastic feeling chordal sounds & single notes will have a more creamy, smooth character. High harmonics created by the gain & controlled largely with TREBLE & PRESENCE, puts a patina of 3D haze on things, that smears with vintage soul. As MID is increased past this region, more thick “gut punch” & low-Treble region attack creeps in & sound becomes more forward.
Be sure to experiment with MID in all gain Modes of Channels 3, paying special attention to feel & sound, it really changes dynamic content & how the strings feel to play.

BASS: Much like MID, this responds like typical Tone control & blends in a fairly wide slice of rich bottom end to round out the sound. Internal switching that occurs when different Modes are selected re-voices both location & freq of bass present for each of the circuits (modes). This difference is crucial to the sounds & big part of their character.

CLEAN & FAT Modes of Channel 1 incorporate a much lower bass freq that adds depth, dimension & air to the sound & needs a much slower taper pot to balance this huge low end with the sounds in the higher gain circuits. Modes in Channels 3 utilize a much higher bass freq, producing a more resonant, thumping quality, keeps things tracking tighter & gives gain sounds a more bouncy alive feel. These higher freqs can be used in greater proportions as compared with the lower & possibly more tone-dangerous freqs used in CLEAN, & FAT modes, as they have less tendency to slow things down or get in the way during faster playing.

Can utilize higher settings of this higher frequency on BASS control in Channel 3 EXTREME Mode, where there’s a huge amount of high-mid/low-treble attack in sound. Try running BASS in 11:00-1:30 range for huge crunch rhythm sounds.

FULL POWER/VARIAC POWER: Performs 2 functions, it determines the flow of AC Power from the wall receptacle & can also be used to switch the entire amp down to a reduced voltage power mode for a looser, more elastic feel. FULL POWER supplies the amp with the full 120v & produces max volume, headroom & punchy bold tone throughout. VARIAC POWER limits incoming AC Voltage to roughly 95v for a “browner” power vibe. This position scoops midrange & has a looser, more elastic feel on the strings, with some shifting (up) of higher harmonics. Can be cool for sounds that rely on output (power amp) clip for their character. Pushed clean, Roots, Blues or Classic Rock Rhythm sounds can all benefit from this softer power feel. When used in conjunction with the 10w power setting, the MkV can deliver the ultimate in saggy, low power performance. For all-around gigging use, we recommend FULL POWER, as this delivers the greatest headroom for clean sounds & most focused/tight-tracking OD sounds.

When using the BIAS SELECT switch on the Rear Panel to accommodate EL34 Power Tubes, switch to VARIAC POWER& operate the amp in this power mode until swapping back to 6L6 Power Tubes. This ensures uninterrupted performance & avoid running EL34s over their rated safe operating voltage.

SWITCHABLE RECTIFIERS: 45W POWER MODE Switchable Rectifiers makes its debut on the MkV in the form of patented Rectifier Tracking. Channels 1 is fitted with toggles that allow you to choose between the tight, bold, higher-headroom response of Silicon DIODES or saggy, sweet, low-output looseness of TUBES (Tube Rectifier) in the 45w Power Mode only. Rectifiers are selected automatically (Solid State) in the 90w & (Tube) in 10w Modes according to their power requirements & associated sound styles. Channel 3 utilizes Silicon Diodes all the time, as the amp circuits it contains all use Silicon Diodes.

DIODES deliver max headroom, attack, dynamic content & track tighter, especially the bass region. They work great for clean chording sounds in Channel 1 & tight-tracking crunch rhythm sounds in Channels 3. Lead sounds are more explosive, focused & deliver greater articulation.

TUBE slows things down, reduces headroom, smooths things out & scoops upper mids & produce a more elastic, bouncy feel on strings. Tube rectification is great for threshold of distortion sounds on rhythm parts & vintage style single note soloing. TUBE also re-voices top end, raising it up an octave & making it a little recessive at the same time.
Info above is from manual, may not correspond directly to AxeFx
“MkV’s basically a collection of previous Mesa amps. May be minor tone differences bc of circuit layout, nothing a few EQ tweaks can’t fix”
“MkV same as MkIV w/ extra features, sounds virtually same”

“Gain control of MkV’s equivalent to OD control on Mk II/IV, actual gain control on Mk V is fixed (same as JPIIC+). In AxeFx, can change Gain control using Ideal tone controls. When choosing the model it’ll be initialized to a value (4.4 for V)”

“On a Mk IV (at least on reference amp) all 3 controls have a Log10A taper. On MkV, tapers are different, so you get more midrange & treble for the same settings. Channel 3 on Mark V is virtually identical to Mark IV Lead channel except for pot tapers”

“I have Mk IIC+, Mk IV, Mk V & Triaxis, all completely different. Mesa says things like “sounds the same as IIC+” but circuits are different & probably most important, knob tapers are completely different”
“Mark series graphic EQ sucks. I know some people want authenticity but it’s simply a bad design”
tips: “Mark series have lots of mids because tonestack is Pre. Can move to post, but will change feel. Pre position is what gives that singing lead tone & sustain. As with real amp, rule of thumb is set bass pretty low. Can add back with EQ after. The kids all do the V EQ, but I use very little. I happen to like lots of mids, makes tone fit in mix better”
“Key to good Boogie sound, IMO, is Fat Switch. This is treble Pull Shift on IIC+ & Pull Fat on Mark IV. Mesa knew this & Lead 2 modes on Triaxis had treble shift engaged by default”

“Tone stack on a Boogie is pre-distortion. Increasing gain, want less bass into distortion stages, idea is to turn bass down. In later Boogie versions (like TriAxis) they changed taper & noon was equivalent to 1 on earlier models, as people are reticent to move controls far from noon”

Turn bright switch on. Every bit of info I’ve found says that people typically used Pull Bright on Volume knob. This is equivalent to Bright switch under Treble control on Block. I always turn it on & I’ve set it on by default for Q2.03.

“USE THE EQ. Tone stack is pre-distortion, atypical for a high-gain amp. Tone stacks almost always post-distortion. Since tone stack is pre-distortion, need to do post distortion tone shaping using EQ. Tone controls set feel & distortion texture, EQ shapes final tone. I like to do a gentle V-curve”
“With presence control at noon, it’s roughly neutral. Turn it down & you’re actually boosting bass & reducing treble”

“For me, MK V with Presence at 10 can be a bit too much “ice pick in forehead” sounding. On Tele it’s most obvious, rolling back tone on guitar helps but still a bit cumbersome. Interestingly, it works great on a Hofner Chancellor Jazz guitar I have. I’ve always had issues balancing this guitar, which tends to be dark & bit boxy (only has PAF style neck pickup). This combo has been very satisfying, low volume from AXE mixed with acoustic adds very nice sheen that’s a direct result of presence at 10 setup (also Pres Shift). Layered MK V with Class A 30W Brilliant using a pedal to transition is also a nice touch to blend in/out sheen” - Forum thread

320.model: MESA/Boogie MkV, Channel 3, IIC+ mode, Bright off
320.controls: Gain, Bass, Mid, Treble, Presence, Master, Normal/Bright, EQ switch
notes: CHANNEL 3 encompasses the best of the MARK Series OD sounds. Beginning with MKIIC+, the sound is pure, blistering focus & the classic Boogie voice of the 80’s, that became the foundation for players like John Petrucci, James Hetfield, Kirk Hammett & a staple for L.A.’s first call session players of the day Steve Lukather, Mike Landau, Dean Parks & many more. Classic “V” curve on Graphic EQ became an integral part of this sound & went on to be the sound of choice for some of the hardest hitting Punk & Hardcore bands of the 90’s/2000’s & still currently used by many top acts. Channel 3 is a faithful recreation of that burning sound of the IIC. MkIV is represented in FAT, where a dose of thick midrange gain is added, combined with a rounding out of upper harmonic peak. Finally EXTREME unleashes all aggression & attack of circuit for a full gain assault that cuts through any mix. (Beware of volume jumps when EXTREME is selected.) NORMAL/BRIGHT switch affects all Modes in CHANNEL 3

While MkV Tone Controls are accurate & effective over a wide range, they come earlier in the signal chain & can only achieve so much shaping before producing possible imbalances in certain Modes. (Ex: Bass Control in Channels 3, where in MkIIC Modes, too much bass dialed early in preamp has a tubby & unfocused sound

The Graphic EQ is at the end of the signal chain, so you can shape the final sound with the only consideration being how much of a certain freq speakers, cabs & your ears can handle. (Extreme settings of 2 lowest Bands, 80Hz & 240Hz use up power quickly & overall headroom is affected)

Channel 3: Overall highest gain in amp & dedicated to creating the best high gain sounds from the fabled MkIIC+ & MkIV. Though the entire channel is aimed at high gain sounds, many expressive/dynamic medium to low-gain sounds can be found here with the GAIN control set lower (below 12:30). Again, this channel defies classification to style & is extremely versatile for both low/high gain, chording & single note sounds.

MkIIC+ is exactly that. This mode is faithful, down to the last detail, recreation of the LEAD Mode of this legendary circuit. Blistering focused gain & explosive attack gives way to morphing harmonics, are it’s soulful signature & after 20 years, these sounds remain at the forefront of Rock. Tight mid-punch focus of this sound provides an open canvas for coloring with the EQ & classic “V” setting is a staple ingredient of the II-C high gain sound for heavy music.

MkIV is a faithful re-creation of the MkIV’s Lead Channel. Because of the vast options in configuring this channel on the MkIV, combined with the fact that the MkIIC+ Mode covers a wide range of brighter sounds, we’ve configured this Mode for a slightly warmer sound. MkIV mode has a big increase in midrange gain, creates the impression of a roll-off in the upper harmonics, resulting in a huge, wide sound, the midrange is voiced higher & stays tighter. Because of this, the EQ does the job of shaping this sound into whatever you want. The EQ doesn’t have to compete with the increased low end early in the preamp of the MkI Mode & can dial in some incredibly big sounds that won’t get flubby.

EXTREME is exactly what it sounds like, extreme & takes it’s architecture from the MkIV, but voiced almost opposite the MkIV mode in this Channel. Forward, aggressive, tight & fast are it’s signature & it is the highest gain/loudest of the MkV’s 9 Modes. Use this mode for crushing impact & stop-on-a-dime dynamics. EXTREME is most suited for heavy styles where max gain & lightning fast attack are the order of the day. Increased sensitivity of the power section in this Mode causes more background noise, as the power amp & driver are “listening harder”. This is normal.

CHANNEL 3 BRIGHT/NORMAL: 2-position switch determines amount of upper harmonics in the sound of all modes of the channel. Some sounds bring forward the action of this switch more than others, depends on amount of top end of the sound to begin with, but it adds or reduces brightness at its location in the signal path in all Modes of this Channel. Ex: you’ll hear its action more in MkIIC+ Mode vs MkIV (FAT) Mode, as the high freqs are more rolled off & recessive in MkIV Mode & therefore there’s less of these freqs present for the BRIGHT switch to bring forward.

In BRIGHT position, sound is infused with upper harmonic halo around note(s) & added top end is more apparent as GAIN is increased, especially in MkIIC+ & EXTREME Modes, where BRIGHT circuit has more highs to work with. BRIGHT position is great for adding harmonic grind to high gain chording sounds in these 2 modes, lets these highs pass at a specific earlier stage in the preamp, the PRESENCE & EQ, can use to blend & shape them later.

In NORMAL position, this region of upper harmonics is rolled off, for a darker, warmer blend that works well for single note soloing. Position is great for adding a feeling of girth & fatness in low gain sounds & removes unwanted sizzle/buzz that can result from low output pickups in high gain settings

The IIC+ mode in Channel 3 uses a smaller coupling cap to deliver the tightest attack & fastest response in the time domain. You also get the bonus of having this mode work incredibly well with the EQ, as the lack of sub-low at the end of the preamp means you can add more low freqs with EQ before the sound gets flubby. So all you IIC & MkIV guys might like this characteristic even better. You can get high gain sounds with the EQ even tighter than ever before

The MkIV & EXTREME Modes utilize a bigger coupling cap, to add sub-low & slow down the attack, for a bigger/fuller slowhand feel that’s huge. Be a little more careful with 80 & 240Hz Sliders when dialing in low end with the EQ, as more low end happens earlier, but the sound is definitely bigger.
If you want it tight, urgent feeling with fastest attack & max focus, use MkIIC+ mode. For the fattest, warmest, biggest sound & don’t need super fast response, use MkIV & EXTREME Modes

Channel 3 is a tribute to the MARK series Channel Switching amps & 3 circuits from the pinnacle of that architecture. 2 most sought after, MkIIC+ & MkIV, responsible for some of the most iconic high gain guitar sounds ever recorded. Channel 3 contains the IIC+ Lead Channel & 2 Modes from MkIV, LEAD & LEAD EXTREME. Has highest gain of the MkV channels, thought of by many as the Lead channel, but there’s many ways to use it. Mid-focus to gain lends itself equally to chording rhythm & single note solo sounds, as it’s articulate, tight-tracking response & lush harmonic layering. These circuits provide amazing resolution across the gain scale with great threshold-of-clip, pushed clean sounds found at the low end of the GAIN control & searing, explosive lead sounds at the high end, with a whole range of urgent, tight crunch rhythm sounds between.

CHANNEL 3 TRIODE/PENTODE: Allows you to choose wiring configuration of the middle pair of power tubes in Channel 3. Feature was popular on the MkIV & changes the personality of the sound’s attack & liquidity in the higher gain condition.

This switch rewires the configuration of the Class A output tube pair (inside 2 6L6’s) to produce a radical sound & feel difference of the modes. Many players like it only one way, saying it makes or breaks the vibe for them or that they can’t play as well when it’s not set to their favorite way. We feel it’s a powerful stylistic parameter & should be explored fully for its usefulness to your sound.

TRIODE softens midrange attack & accentuates the upper harmonic region, creating a silky, more compressed, almost liquid feel & lowers overall power output. This tends to raise the harmonic haze, sweetens top end & it shines for expressive high gain solo work or high gain chording that’s more textural than rhythmic. It offers more complexity & nuance, but trade-off is it may not cut through a mix as well. TRIODE produces less overall power output so it’s probably not the choice for very low gain chording, unless you’re looking for more of a “vintage sag” feel. Original MkIIC+ amps were hard-wired to TRIODE. MkIV offered a choice between the 2 configurations.

PENTODE accentuates midrange punch & lowers the upper harmonic region for a bolder, tighter attack, especially in the low end & increases output power & headroom. It has more immediate dynamics, with greater peaks & feels “faster” to play, almost anticipating your next input. This urgent attack means PENTODE excels at any style, where rhythmic nuance & tight-tracking accuracy are essential. May be the best choice for solo sounds that pop through a mix & defined/articulate high gain crunch chording, with huge tight low-end.

BIAS SELECT: Allows for proper biasing when swapping to EL34 type power tubes, for a brighter, harmonic-laden response. It selects a different set of bias resistors & insures these extremely different power tubes will sound better & work more reliably.

MkIIC+: Recreation of the sought after sound of these 2-channel MARK series amps, produced in the mid 80s that became the voice of choice for many recording artists of the day. The tone is identical, except the Sylvania 415 power tubes, which are no longer available. During R&D, we even found ways to mimic the important mid-punch character inherent in those tubes & far better, you don’t have to compromise your clean or lead sound, because they share controls like in the original layout! The IIC+ trademark sound is urgent & stripped, but also has incredible focus despite it’s precious multi-dimensional layers of upper harmonics. It works equally well for aggressive high gain chording & blistering single note soloing in low or high regions of the GAIN control. When dialed in (GAIN 1:30-2:30, TREBLE 12:00-1:00, BASS 10:00-12:00, PRESENCE 9:00-11:30), it has a lead voice that’s unrivaled in articulation, nuance & time domain accuracy in high gain genres. These qualities are especially favored by those players whose technical ability demands instantaneous response & tight, detailed tracking of pick attack. After the attack, a beautiful morphing of harmonics occurs & notes segue through a whole range of dynamic & freq changes that’s a joy to experience. You’ll find yourself playing like never before & reaching newfound depths of expression.

For high gain rhythm work, IIC+ unleashes the other sound in Heavy Rock Crunch. More complex & harmonically layered than its British fueled counterpart, the C+ comes on like a grinding wall of gain, that is truly menacing. The shameless scooping of mids & rebellious boosting of both lows & highs simultaneously led to the iconic “V” curve becoming so popular in the 80s recordings, that it became synonymous with the IIC+ sound. This sound reached further notoriety & became referred to as Boogie Crunch & even the “California Sound”.

Through the 90s, our Dual Rectifier’s sub-low enhanced grind & punishing blend of attack & harmonics became the pop-metal sound. However, there remained a strong cult following for the MARK Series/Graphic EQ crunch sound ( re-introduced in the MkIV) & this tighter, more articulate sound is now a classic & here to stay. In the current decade, it’s become the crunch of choice for high tempo aggressive Punk & Indie Rock, chosen once again for its’ ability to stay glued to pick attack & track even at burning tempos.

There are no real danger zones or pitfalls with the C+ mode, other than the obvious, turn the BASS control down slightly in proportion to increase of GAIN. Don’t try to run the GAIN maxed out with TREBLE &/or PRESENCE way up, as preamp tubes will most likely not handle this abuse & begin to show their individual degree of microphonicity
Hints for the C+ Mode might include these:
Use the Graphic EQ for extreme low end with high GAIN settings, it comes later in the circuit & will have less tendency to get loose & flubby vs BASS control.

Work with GAIN, TREBLE & PRESENCE in finite increments when searching for your ideal lead voice, as these interact greatly & have a big effect on pick attack sensitivity & focus. PRESENCE compresses things in its lower regions creating a more voice-like character & opens up the upper harmonic region in higher settings, for a more cutting, blade-like attack.
For lead sounds, Roll in BASS wanted after fine-tuning the attack signature with GAIN, TREBLE & PRESENCE.
Fill things in just enough, but don’t create flub. The BASS control brings in beautiful rich low end, but can overtake the balance set by the other controls quickly & degrade attack.

Don’t overlook this Mode for lower gain sounds! Because of the harmonic content & instant attack properties, it excels at low gain Blues sounds, both rhythm/single note & can produce some threshold of clip, almost clean sounds. It’s open, dynamic & responds great to plucking techniques too. Traditionalists have even commented on how well the old “guitar volume knob” or “oldschool channel switching” approach works with this sound. Set low enough, C+ works great just backing off for clean & cranking up for lead on the guitars’ Volume pot. When GAIN is this low, you can dial in more BASS to add warmth & 3-dimensionality.

This is an addicting mode to play & one of, if not the most expressive, of the 9 Modes. Spend some quality time exploring how the controls interact, once you dial it in for your individual style, magic will happen.

MARK IV: In comparison to the MkIIC+ mode, the MkIV mode is infused with more low mid & has an attack character that’s wider & less pointed in the upper mids, bottom end goes down lower & has more gain too, giving the sound thickness & girth, that produces huge, ominous crunch chords & smooth vocal single note sounds. Circuit differences create a different feel, it feels creamier & gives impression of less resistance on the strings, making it easier to play for many guitarists. Slightly less-instantaneous attack created by the addition of low end makes the IV Mode feel a little slower & less like your picking technique is ”under the microscope” & can be either freedom or lack of definition, depending on your POV & stylistic needs.

For lower gain sounds, MkIV mode has more air & 3-dimensionality vs C+. Some nice purring threshold-of-clip sounds can be found with GAIN set very low (9:00-10:00) & TREBLE around 12:30. With GAIN this low, you can dial in quite a bit of BASS (11:00-1:30) before things get too tubby, letting you really move some air. Here’s also a great place to experiment with both TRIODE/PENTODE &/or POWER MODES. PENTODE will produce a bold, punchy sound that will let you jab with authority.

High gain sounds in the IV Mode are fat! The lower bass freqs combined with added low mid gain makes for the biggest crunch chording sounds in the amp. Watch setting BASS more carefully, as lower freqs bottom end can get bloated much faster. If looking for huge bottom end with high gain settings, it’s wise to turn to the EQ to achieve this. BASS dumps too much sub-low into the signal path, at a point earlier in the preamp. It gets amplified over & over, until it turns to flub, whereas the EQ comes at the end of the signal chain & adds low end to the “finished preamp sound”.

NORMAL/BRIGHT switch is very effective at bringing forward upper harmonics, especially for high gain chording & even single note sounds. When adding this upper-stratosphere layer of tone by engaging BRIGHT, it may be necessary to reduce PRESENCE (which contains a narrower, adjustable band of these highs) in order to arrive at the sound that’s right for you. Some people are very sensitive to these upper highs, heard as edgy, buzzy & unpleasant. For those players, NORMAL position provided to notch them out almost completely. We feel they’re an important part of the spectrum, as they give the sound spacial width, openness & a beautiful layer of stacked harmonics. However, they must be blended in as an integral part of the sound.

Can be achieved in a number of ways once you’ve decided to include this region of the spectrum with BRIGHT, such as the Tone Controls, EQ, TRIODE/PENTODE, the speaker cab & finally, a big component often overlooked, their guitar & its pickups. Even their own individual picking/fingering technique & the gauge of strings they use, all of these factors affect the type & amount of high harmonics that can be introduced & still sound balanced, an integrated tone, rather than shrill or annoying.

Pickups are a huge factor in the overall tonal character. Many players stick with 1 instrument & if they have trouble dialing in a sound on their amp, they overlook the fact that the sound begins & is largely defined by, what’s sent to the amp from their instrument. High gain sounds are especially sensitive to output/voicing of pickups & even more so, to the amount of high end that’s emphasized. Weaker, more vintage style pickups, accentuate upper harmonics & are wonderful for shimmering, bell-like harmonics & clarity in low to medium gain applications. When you’re looking for higher gain performance, these types of pickups present some challenges, as those upper harmonics can get buzzy & thin sounding as gain increases. You will likely find it necessary to roll TREBLE & PRESENCE back substantially when searching for a high gain sound that’s focused & pure with these pickups.

If high gain is your bag, you’ve probably already come to the conclusion that you need a fairly high output pickup, at least in the bridge position, to achieve the tight focus needed to produce cohesive high gain sounds. If not, may we suggest you try several different higher output pickups, which tend to put emphasis on the mids & higher midrange, as opposed to top end. This voicing difference will produce tighter low end for crunch chords & a more voice-like single note sound.

Some higher output pickups will have taps, or can be tapped, at a halfway point in the winding, giving the best of both worlds, a weaker output/brighter tap & the full winding, high output/punchier mid setting. This is usually controlled via a toggle or pull pot, but can also be hard-wired to a specific position on a standard 5-way or toggle. This is a great way to have the most versatility possible & keep high harmonic content & openness for your low to mid gain applications & then be able to switch your guitar, along with the Channels of the MkV, to a high output/high gain machine, capable of tight, ferocious heavy sounds.

EXTREME: The last Channel 3 mode is named appropriately & is all about more! More gain, more attack, more punishing mids, more tight, huge lows & more output volume. EXTREME traces its lineage back to a feature on the MkIV that resided on the Channel 3 (LEAD) PRESENCE control of that amp. A pull-pot fitted there allowed removal of negative feedback from the power section & unleashed the pent-up fury of the Simul-Class output.

This feature allows the power section Presence circuit to respond to all freqs more equally, instead of a chosen adjustable set of high freqs & removes an element of “control” & inherent compression in the power amp. This wider EQ curve in the rear end creates a rebellious, unleashed & extremely open personality that can’t be duplicated with front end preamp circuitry. When this radically aggressive power personality is combined with the high gain wall of layered harmonics in the MkIV mode, a sound of truly stunning proportions is created.

Top end has been warmed, low end has been tightened & feel improved, making EXTREME in the V easier to play & even more expressive vs its’ predecessor. The attack, body, girth & versatility of the V’s EXTREME Mode will allow you to wield this power in more places for more styles, even venturing into some lower gain uses the IV dare not go.

Many Hard Core devotees love the way the EXTREME Mode can handle very high settings of the GAIN control & still retain attack & tightness of high gain chording. It’s not even necessary to run TREBLE high to achieve this tightness & settings in 12:00-1:00 range are common. Remember that for very high gain chording, it’s better to set BASS lower (10:00-11:00) & look for additional low end via the EQ, as bottom end introduced late in the signal chain stays tighter longer that its’ early preamp counterpart.

As mentioned, some urgent, packing-an-attitude lower gain sounds are possible when EXTREME’s used with lower GAIN settings. For these types of sounds you can increase BASS (11:30-1:30) to add 3D warmth, since there’s less gain dialed & less chance of causing unwanted flub.

There will seem a slight decrease in the power of PRESENCE in EXTREME, as negative feedback has been radically reduced in a broad range of freqs, including those chosen for the PRESENCE circuit, which means there’s less for the narrow band affected by PRESENCE to work on. This isn’t an issue, as there are plenty of highs available on TREBLE & top bands of the EQ to make the sound as bright as needed.
For more vintage sounds with lower gain settings, try TRIODE, for a more bouncy, sweet & harmonically rich voice with fair amount of old school sag to the power.

For authority, punch & tight-tracking low end, try PENTODE with very high GAIN settings. This produces a more immediate attack response, deliver the most power & headroom to handle huge lows associated with these styles.
For these settings & styles you don’t want any “vintage sag” slowing down response & loosening low end, PENTODE will ensure power stays stiff & instantaneous.
IIC+ & MkIV owners, if you end up doing a side by side with a IIC+ for the LEAD Mode, use IIC+ & MkV set like this for fair comparison:
SET IIC+ As Follows:
VOLUME control Pulled (Bright On) & set to Approx. 7 ¾. (This stage in MkV is set to a sweet spot we found)
LEAD DRIVE Control Pulled & set to desired setting
All Tone Controls set by ear as close as possible (we measure each pot & set both exactly with an ohm meter).
PRESENCE set to desired setting. (0 or 10 is most fair for comparisons sake & removes pot variance)
GRAPHIC EQ Off (Bypassed)
SET MARK V As Follows:
GAIN set by ear & relative “clock face” setting to IIC LEAD DRIVE.
Tone Controls set by ear & relative “clock face” setting as IIC tone controls. (IIC BASS is 2nd position/MID 3rd & MkV is T/M/B)
Channel 3 BRIGHT switch in BRIGHT position.
Channel 3 TRIODE/PENTODE switch set to TRIODE
SET MARK IV As Follows:
Channel 3 (LEAD)
LEAD GAIN Pulled & set to 7 ¾. LEAD DRIVE Pulled/set as desired
Channel 3 (LEAD) Tone Controls set as desired
Pull All ctrls, unless comparing EXTREME (leave LEAD PRES In)
PRESENCE as desired (0 or 10 most fair & removes pot variance)
TRIODE/PENTODE switch set to PENTODE
Set MARK V As Follows:
Channel 3 set to MkIV or EXTREME Mode (Set same as MkIV)
GAIN matches “clock face” setting of LEAD DRIVE setting on MkIV
Chnl3 tone controls set to match relative clockface settings on MkIV
Channel 3 BRIGHT/NORMAL switch set to BRIGHT
Channel 3 PRESENCE set to relative setting on MkIV
TRIODE/PENTODE switch set to PENTODE

Comparisons are close as possible of setting & configuration of circuits. Doing these tests, important to account for power tubes, preamp tubes, transformers & even caps & resistors may be different depending on availability at time of construction
Info above is from manual, may not correspond directly to AxeFx

notes: “That little JCM800 Studio is a cool amp, doesn’t sound like its big brothers, but has its own thing going on that’s interesting. Sorta like Marshall meets Vox.”
See 046 Brit 800 for more info
“They’re simple amps with minimal tone shaping”
Original amp is a 25w Class A, has all-tube warmth & power, plus analog spring reverb, 2-band EQ & master volume
Power amp has custom output transformer with 16ohm, 8ohm & 4ohm output options. Has phenomenal touch sensitivity & bite
Has Jensen P12Q, 1x12 Deluxe Tweed DynaCab is a good match
Brownface 6G3, Bright channel

Fat switch controls value of a capacitor in tone stack. 6G3 doesn’t have a tone stack, so switch isn’t applicable. Bright switch & Bright cap control value of a capacitor across Drive pot. 6G3 doesn’t have a conventional drive circuit, so these aren’t applicable

For guitarists hip to what came in between, brown-panel 6G3 of ‘61-’63 is one of tastiest tone machines of bunch, packing best-of-both-worlds sounds that can twang, jangle, sparkle & roar, depending on how you attack it.

With 2 full gain stages before the phase inverter & those derived from a 7025 (aka 12AX7) preamp tube vs lower-gain 12AY7 of tweeds & very little signal loss from passive tone control, circuit can push hot signal into output stage

Amp’s back end was further altered from tweed-Deluxe template. More complex long-tailed-pair phase inverter for hifi response, more efficient fixed-bias setup for 2 6V6GTs/GZ34s firmer rectification tube (vs 5E3’s 5Y3 valve).
Put it all together & you get meaty vintage-style OD from preamp cranked to throaty roar by output stage, for lead tones many compare to mini Marshall with American twist

Has tremolo effect predecessor never had. Powered by ½ of 2nd of 3 12AX7 in preamp, bias-modulating circuit applies its modulation to output tubes’ bias network. One of simpler tube-trem circuits ever, but a rich/warm sound

Many earlier examples of 6G3 came with highly regarded 12” Jensen P12Q speakers with Alnico magnets, but by the time of this Deluxe’s ‘62 release, Oxford 12K5 became standard issue. Still a good-sounding speaker & makes crisp delivery of what 6G3 has to offer when amp is kept at low-to-medium volumes
